prompts.title: Multi-region sliding-window rate limiter
prompts.text:
ACME Payments fronts its public API with gateways in five regions: us-east, us-west, eu-central, ap-southeast, sa-east. Peak aggregate traffic is 2,000,000 requests/second split 38 / 17 / 24 / 16 / 5 percent across those regions respectively. There are 4.2 million active API keys; the top 0.1% of keys account for 62% of traffic.

Design the global rate limiter. Hard requirements:

- Per-key quotas are GLOBAL, not per-region. A key with a 10,000 req/min quota must not spend more than 10,000 in any 60-second sliding window summed across all regions. Sustained overshoot above 2% is a contract violation; transient overshoot during the 30-second cross-region convergence budget is acceptable.
- The limiter decision must add no more than 5 ms to p99 request latency and no more than 0.9 ms to p50, measured at the gateway.
- Quotas are tiered: 47% of keys are on a 600 req/min tier, 51% on 10,000 req/min, 1.8% on 250,000 req/min, and 0.2% are 'enterprise' with per-endpoint quotas (up to 40 distinct endpoint buckets per key).
- During a full region partition (a region can reach clients but not other regions) the partitioned region must keep serving. State what limiting behaviour it adopts and justify the safety/availability trade you are making.
- Quota changes made in the control plane must take effect everywhere within 30 seconds.

Deliverables, in this order:

1. Architecture. Components, where counters live, the exact read/write path for an allowed request and for a denied request. Say explicitly which hop is on the critical path and which is asynchronous.
2. Algorithm. Pick the counting scheme (fixed window, sliding window log, sliding window counter, token bucket, or a hybrid) and defend it against the 2% overshoot bound. Show the worst-case overshoot arithmetic for your choice, not a hand-wave.
3. Capacity math. Compute: bytes of state per key per window; total resident memory for the counter tier and how many nodes that implies at 64 GiB usable per node; cross-region replication bandwidth in Mbit/s at steady state (state your batching interval and per-message overhead assumptions); and QPS per shard given your shard count. Show every intermediate number.
4. Hot-key handling. The top key sustains 90,000 req/s alone. Explain how a single logical counter survives that without becoming a hotspot, and quantify the extra overshoot your mitigation introduces.
5. Failure modes. Enumerate at least seven, each with detection signal, blast radius, and mitigation: counter-tier node loss, full region partition, control-plane outage, clock skew of 400 ms between regions, replication lag spike to 90 s, a poisoned quota config push, and cold start of a region after 20 minutes down.
6. Rejected alternatives. At least four, each with the specific number or property that killed it: a single global Redis cluster, per-region static quota slicing, a consensus (Raft) counter per key, and one more of your choosing. Do not merely say 'too slow'; give the latency or cost figure.
7. A rollout plan that can be aborted, and the three metrics you would page on.

Be numerically concrete throughout. If you need an assumption (packet size, RTT between regions, serialization overhead) state it as an explicit assumption line before you use it.

prompts.title: Cross-cloud idempotent payment ledger
prompts.text:
A payments company must run its core double-entry ledger across three clouds simultaneously (AWS us-east-1, GCP us-central1, Azure eastus2) because a single-provider outage in the last fiscal year cost it a regulatory finding. Write the design.

Workload and constraints:
- 40,000 ledger transactions/second at peak, each touching between 2 and 11 accounts. Mean 3.4 postings per transaction.
- Every transaction must be exactly-once with respect to money movement. Client retries are frequent: 4.1% of requests are retries carrying the same idempotency key, and 0.3% carry the same key with a DIFFERENT body (client bug). Both cases must be handled and the second must be an error, not a silent no-op.
- Balances must never go negative for accounts flagged no_overdraft (63% of accounts). This is a cross-row invariant checked at commit time.
- Regulatory: an immutable audit record for every posting, retained 7 years, queryable by account within 3 seconds for the last 90 days and within 5 minutes for older data.
- RPO = 0 for committed transactions. RTO <= 90 seconds for loss of one entire cloud.
- p99 commit latency budget: 250 ms end to end from client.
- Account count: 380 million. 92% of accounts see fewer than 5 transactions/month; the top 4,000 accounts (merchant settlement accounts) see up to 3,000 postings/second each.

Produce:

1. The consistency model you commit to and why it satisfies both RPO=0 and the 250 ms p99. If you use a consensus protocol, name it, state the quorum shape across three clouds, and compute the expected commit latency using inter-cloud RTTs you state up front. If you do NOT use cross-cloud consensus on the hot path, explain precisely how you still get RPO=0.
2. Sharding scheme, including what happens to a transaction that spans two shards. Give the distributed-commit mechanism and its failure handling, including the in-doubt window and how long a lock can be held.
3. The idempotency subsystem: key format, storage, TTL, how you detect same-key-different-body, and what the ledger does if the idempotency record commits but the ledger commit does not (and vice versa). Draw the state machine.
4. Hot merchant accounts: 3,000 postings/second against one balance row will serialize. Give a concrete technique (and the reconciliation job it implies) that preserves the no_overdraft invariant. Quantify the worst-case staleness of the visible balance.
5. Capacity math: storage per posting including audit copy; total bytes/day and bytes/7-years; IOPS required; index sizes; and the cost delta of tri-cloud versus single-cloud expressed as a multiplier with the reasoning behind each factor.
6. Failure modes table, at least eight rows: one cloud gone, network partition isolating two clouds from the third, clock skew, a shard leader flapping, silent data corruption in one replica, an operator running a bad migration, duplicate delivery from the upstream queue, and a poison transaction that crashes the apply path.
7. Rejected alternatives, minimum five, each with the disqualifying number: single-region Postgres with cross-cloud async replicas, Kafka-as-ledger with compaction, event sourcing with CQRS read models only, Spanner/CockroachDB multi-cloud, and a saga-based eventual ledger.
8. What you would deliberately NOT build in v1, and the exact risk you are accepting.

prompts.title: Collaborative editing backend
prompts.text:
Specify the server side of a real-time collaborative document editor competing with Google Docs. Numbers you must design against:

- 500,000 documents open concurrently at peak; 1.9 million connected clients (mean 3.8 editors per open doc, but the distribution is heavy-tailed: 0.4% of docs have more than 200 simultaneous editors, max observed 4,100).
- Median document 42 KB of text plus 180 KB of structural metadata; p99 document 14 MB.
- Median keystroke-to-remote-echo latency must be under 120 ms for editors in the same continent, under 320 ms cross-continent, measured p95.
- Offline editing supported for up to 30 days, then merge. Merges must never lose a user's text, and must never produce interleaved garbage inside a word.
- Full version history with the ability to restore any 30-second checkpoint from the last 180 days.
- Documents may be shared with permission changes taking effect within 2 seconds, including revocation mid-session.

Work through the following:

1. Concurrency control. Choose between operational transformation and a CRDT family (state-based, op-based, RGA/Logoot/Yjs-style, or a text-specific structure). Justify with respect to the offline-30-days requirement and the 4,100-editor document. State the metadata overhead your choice imposes per character and compute the in-memory size of the p99 document under it. If tombstones accumulate, give the garbage-collection protocol and prove it is safe for a client that has been offline 29 days.
2. Session and connection tier. How 1.9 million websockets are distributed, what happens on process restart, and how a document's authoritative state is pinned to exactly one place (or why it does not need to be). Give the failover sequence and the worst-case editing stall in milliseconds.
3. Persistence. Log-of-operations versus snapshotting cadence; the arithmetic for choosing the cadence given the 180-day/30-second checkpoint requirement, including total stored bytes for 500k active docs.
4. The 4,100-editor document. Naive fan-out is 4,100 x 4,100 message pairs. Give the fan-out topology, the batching/coalescing rule and its latency cost, and compute the egress bandwidth for that single doc at 2 edits/second/editor.
5. Permission revocation. Explain how a mid-session revoke is enforced within 2 s without a per-operation authorization round trip, and what an adversarial client can still observe in the gap.
6. Failure modes: split-brain on document ownership, a client that replays stale operations, a corrupted CRDT state that crashes every peer that loads it, a rogue client generating 50,000 ops/second, and storage write amplification.
7. Rejected alternatives, at least four, with the specific disqualifying property. Include a plain last-writer-wins design and a lock-per-paragraph design.
8. A test strategy that could actually catch a convergence bug before production, described concretely enough to implement.

prompts.title: Point-in-time correct feature store
prompts.text:
Our fraud models keep degrading in production and the postmortems all say the same thing: training/serving skew. Build the feature platform that makes that class of bug structurally impossible, and be specific enough that an engineer could start writing code from your document.

Environment:
- 2,400 features across 61 feature groups. 380 of them are streaming aggregations (e.g. 'count of declined authorizations for this card in the last 15 minutes'), 1,600 are batch-computed daily, the rest are on-demand transforms of the request payload.
- Online serving: 90,000 inferences/second, each needing 140 to 900 features. p99 feature-fetch budget is 18 ms for the whole vector.
- Offline training sets: up to 4 billion rows x 900 features, rebuilt weekly, must be point-in-time correct to the millisecond of the labelled event.
- Raw event volume: 210 TB/year. Feature values retained 25 months for training.
- Backfills happen constantly; a new feature must be backfillable over 25 months of history in under 6 hours.

Answer in this structure:

1. The data model. Define entity keys, feature vectors, event timestamps versus processing timestamps, and the exact join semantics that guarantee point-in-time correctness. Write the join as pseudo-SQL and explain why a naive equijoin on date is wrong; give a concrete example row where the naive join leaks future information.
2. Storage layout. Online store and offline store: pick technologies, state the row/column layout, key encoding, and compute storage volume for both. Show the arithmetic for the online store working set at 90k QPS with 900 features per request, including serialization format overhead.
3. Latency budget. Break the 18 ms p99 into hops with a number on each. If your design needs more than one round trip per inference, justify it or eliminate it.
4. Streaming aggregations. The 15-minute windowed counters must be identical in training and serving. Explain how you compute them offline over history and online in real time WITHOUT writing the logic twice, and what you do about late-arriving events (state your allowed lateness and its effect on correctness).
5. Backfill. Show that the 6-hour target is reachable: parallelism, bytes scanned, shuffle volume, cost. If it is not reachable with your design, say so and change the design.
6. Failure modes: a streaming job restarting and double-counting, a schema change to an upstream topic, a feature whose upstream table silently stops updating, clock skew between producers, and a training run that reads a partially-written partition. For each, give the detection mechanism (be specific: which metric, which threshold).
7. Rejected alternatives, at least four, including 'just recompute features from raw logs at training time' and 'log the served feature vector and train on that' (this one is tempting; explain both what it buys and exactly what it costs).
8. The three invariants you would enforce in CI to prevent skew regressions.

prompts.title: Service discovery without DNS
prompts.text:
Our platform team has concluded that DNS-based service discovery is the root cause of four of our last six SEV-1s (negative caching, TTL disrespect by client libraries, resolver overload, and a stale record served for 11 minutes after a failover). Replace it.

Scale and constraints:
- 80,000 pods across 340 clusters in 14 regions. Median pod lifetime 6 hours; p10 lifetime is 90 seconds (batch jobs). Peak churn is 900 endpoint changes/second globally, bursting to 14,000/second during a cluster drain.
- 1,900 logical services. The largest has 6,200 endpoints; the median has 9.
- A caller must observe an endpoint removal within 3 seconds of the endpoint being marked unhealthy, and must NEVER send traffic to an endpoint that has been gone for more than 10 seconds.
- The discovery system must survive its own control plane being completely down for 30 minutes with no data-plane impact for steady-state traffic.
- Clients are polyglot: Go, Java, Python, Rust, and one legacy C++ service that cannot be recompiled.

Deliver:

1. The protocol. Push or pull, transport, incremental versus full state, and the exact wire semantics for add/remove/update. Define the versioning/nonce scheme that makes updates idempotent and lets a client detect that it missed an update.
2. The 6,200-endpoint service. Compute the bytes of a full state push, the bytes of an incremental push at 900 changes/second, and the total egress from a control-plane node serving 5,000 subscribers. Then explain how you keep that number sane (deduplication, delta encoding, subscriber sharding) and show the improved arithmetic.
3. Health. Who decides an endpoint is unhealthy: the control plane, the client, or both? Design for the case where they disagree. Give the outlier-ejection rule with concrete thresholds and explain how you prevent an ejection cascade that removes every endpoint of a service.
4. The legacy C++ client that cannot be recompiled. Give a migration path with no flag day.
5. Control-plane outage. Show, step by step, why steady-state traffic is unaffected for 30 minutes, and enumerate exactly which operations become impossible during that window.
6. Consistency. Two callers can hold different views of the same service. Bound the divergence and explain what breaks if a request is routed to an endpoint that a peer already considers dead (idempotency? retries? connection draining?).
7. Failure modes: control-plane split brain, a subscriber that never acks, a bad config that empties a service, thundering herd on control-plane restart with 80,000 pods reconnecting, and a cluster whose kubelet reports 14,000 changes/second due to a crashloop.
8. Rejected alternatives with the disqualifying number: DNS with 1s TTL, a gossip mesh (SWIM) among all 80,000 pods, a shared etcd watched by every pod, and client-side static config with deploy-time templating.
9. The rollback story if the new system is worse than DNS.

prompts.title: Metrics ingestion at 18M samples/s
prompts.text:
You have inherited a metrics platform that is falling over. Redesign it end to end.

Current state and targets:
- Ingest 18,000,000 samples/second sustained, 31,000,000 at peak (a sample is a (series_id, timestamp, float64) triple; series_id is derived from a metric name plus label set).
- Active series: 640 million in the last 2 hours. Total distinct series seen in 30 days: 9.4 billion. This is the problem: a team shipped a label containing a request UUID and created 2.1 billion series in 40 minutes.
- Retention: raw 10-second resolution for 15 days, 1-minute rollup for 90 days, 5-minute rollup for 400 days, 1-hour rollup for 5 years.
- Query SLO: dashboard queries touching <= 50,000 series over 6 hours must return p99 in 1.5 s. Alerting queries (12,000 rules, evaluated every 30 s) must never be starved by dashboard queries.
- Writes must not be lost during a rolling restart of the ingest tier.

Produce:

1. Ingest path. Protocol, batching, the exact sharding key, and how you avoid a hot shard when one service emits 40% of all samples. Compute samples/second/node and the network bytes/second/node under your batching and compression assumptions (state them).
2. Storage. Choose the on-disk format and justify it with compression arithmetic: show bytes-per-sample for timestamps and values under delta-of-delta plus XOR encoding, then compute total bytes for 15 days of raw data. Compare against a naive 16-bytes-per-sample layout and give the ratio.
3. Cardinality control. Design the mechanism that would have stopped the 2.1-billion-series incident within 60 seconds. It must be automatic, must not drop the innocent metrics of an innocent team, and must be explainable to the team that got limited. Give the detection statistic, the threshold, the enforcement action, and the false-positive analysis.
4. Rollups. Where they are computed (ingest-time, background compaction, or query-time), how you handle late samples arriving after a rollup has been sealed, and the exact semantics for counters that reset. Show why a naive average-of-averages is wrong for a 5-minute rollup built from 1-minute rollups and give the correct approach.
5. Query engine. Index structure for label matching (be specific: inverted index posting lists, their size, and intersection strategy), the memory bound per query, and the isolation mechanism that protects the 12,000 alerting rules from a single pathological dashboard query. Give the admission-control numbers.
6. Capacity model. Total nodes for ingest, storage, and query, with the arithmetic. Include replication factor and the resulting cost multiplier.
7. Failure modes, at least seven, including: an ingest node losing its write-ahead log, compaction falling permanently behind, a query that OOMs a storage node, clock skew producing out-of-order samples, and a customer replaying 3 days of buffered data at 20x speed after their network heals.
8. Rejected alternatives with numbers: a single Prometheus per cluster with federation, storing every sample in Cassandra, an OLAP columnar warehouse as the primary store, and a fully in-memory tier.

prompts.title: Multi-tenant vector search platform
prompts.text:
Product wants a hosted vector search service. I want the design document. Constraints are non-negotiable; if one is unachievable, prove it and propose the closest achievable variant.

- 4.1 billion vectors total, 768 dimensions, float32 on ingest. 11,000 tenants. Tenant size distribution: median 40,000 vectors, p95 3.2 million, largest single tenant 900 million.
- Query load: 26,000 queries/second aggregate. p99 latency 120 ms including network, for top-50 retrieval with a metadata filter that eliminates 0 to 99.9% of a tenant's corpus.
- Recall@50 must be at least 0.94 versus exact search, measured per tenant, and must be reported honestly to tenants.
- Writes: 180,000 upserts/second aggregate; a newly written vector must be searchable within 5 seconds. Deletes must take effect within 5 seconds (this is a GDPR requirement, not a nicety).
- Hard multi-tenant isolation: no tenant may ever see another's vector or infer its existence via timing.
- Cost target: under 1.1 cents per 1,000 queries at steady state.

Required sections:

1. Index choice. Compare HNSW, IVF-PQ, IVF-Flat, and DiskANN/Vamana style graph-on-SSD for THIS workload. Decide, and back it with memory arithmetic: compute resident bytes/vector for each candidate at 768 dims (state the quantization scheme, the codebook size, and the graph degree you assume), then total RAM for 4.1 billion vectors under each. Show the numbers, then pick.
2. The 5-second freshness requirement conflicts with graph index build cost. Resolve it. Describe the write path, the delta/segment structure, the merge policy, and the query-time fan-out across immutable segments plus the mutable head. Quantify the recall and latency cost of searching N segments and pick N.
3. Filtered search. A 99.9%-selective metadata filter breaks ANN graph traversal (you may find no candidates). Explain the failure precisely, then give your strategy (pre-filtering, post-filtering with over-fetch, filter-aware traversal, or partitioned indexes) with the crossover analysis: at what filter selectivity do you switch strategies, and how do you estimate selectivity at query time?
4. Tenancy. How the 900-million-vector tenant and the 40,000-vector tenant coexist without either wasting resources or being noisy neighbours. Give the placement algorithm and the rebalancing trigger. Explain the timing-side-channel defence concretely.
5. Deletes in 5 seconds against an immutable segment format. Give the mechanism, its query-time cost, and the compaction schedule that keeps that cost bounded. Compute worst-case tombstone ratio before compaction must run.
6. Capacity and cost. Nodes, RAM, SSD, replication, and the derivation of cost per 1,000 queries. If you cannot hit 1.1 cents, say what it actually costs and which constraint to relax.
7. Failure modes: a segment merge that corrupts a graph, recall silently degrading after a bad quantizer retrain, a tenant issuing 200k QPS, an OOM during merge, and node loss with 900 million vectors on it (state the recovery time).
8. Rejected alternatives, at least four, each with the number that killed it. Include brute-force GPU search and 'one Postgres+pgvector per tenant'.

prompts.title: Deadline-aware transcoding on spot capacity
prompts.text:
Build the video transcoding pipeline for a user-generated-content platform. The interesting part is that most of the compute must come from preemptible/spot instances, and the deadlines are contractual.

Workload:
- 310,000 uploads/day, log-normal duration: median 3.1 minutes, p90 14 minutes, p99 96 minutes, maximum 6 hours. Mean source bitrate 12 Mbit/s.
- Every upload is transcoded into 7 renditions (240p through 4K) plus 3 audio tracks plus thumbnail sprites plus a 6-second preview loop.
- Two SLA classes. 'Creator Pro' (9% of uploads) must have the 720p rendition playable within 4 minutes of upload completion and all renditions within 20 minutes. Standard uploads must complete all renditions within 3 hours, p99.
- Spot capacity is 30-70% cheaper but can be reclaimed with 30 seconds notice; historical reclamation rate is 4.2% of instance-hours, clustered (when it happens, it often takes 20-40% of a fleet in one region within 5 minutes).
- Budget: median cost per upload must be under 3.4 cents.

Write the design:

1. Job decomposition. Explain chunked (segment-parallel) transcoding: how you split, what you do about GOP boundaries and scene-change alignment, how you stitch, and why naive fixed-duration splitting produces visible artifacts or bitrate spikes at the seams. Compute the parallelism achievable on a 96-minute p99 video and the resulting wall-clock time.
2. Scheduler. This is the core. Design a deadline-aware scheduler over a heterogeneous, preempting fleet. Define the priority function explicitly (as a formula), the admission control, and the mechanism that guarantees the 4-minute Creator Pro 720p target even when the spot fleet loses 40% of its capacity. State how much on-demand capacity you keep as a floor and derive that number from the reclamation statistics above.
3. Preemption handling. What happens to a chunk in flight at the 30-second notice; checkpointing versus restart; the arithmetic for whether checkpointing is worth it given mean chunk duration. Show the expected wasted-work calculation both ways.
4. Capacity math. Compute total transcode-seconds/day (state your assumed encoding speed ratio per rendition, e.g. x264 preset throughput in realtime multiples), convert to vCPU-hours, then to instances, then to dollars, and check it against the 3.4-cent target. Show every step. If it fails, adjust a rendition ladder or encoder setting and redo the number.
5. Storage and egress. Intermediate chunk storage volume, lifecycle policy, and egress cost. Include the cost of a failed job's orphaned artifacts and the cleanup mechanism.
6. Failure modes: a corrupt source that crashes the decoder (and its retry storm), a rendition that silently produces black frames, a stitching bug that only manifests on variable-frame-rate sources, region-wide spot exhaustion, queue backlog growth that is only detectable 40 minutes before SLA breach, and a poison job that is retried forever.
7. Backpressure. Define exactly when you start rejecting or degrading, what you degrade first, and how you tell the user.
8. Rejected alternatives, minimum four, with numbers: all on-demand, a third-party transcoding API, per-file (non-chunked) transcoding, and GPU-only encoding.

prompts.title: CDC fan-out with schema evolution
prompts.text:
Sixty-one microservices currently read directly from a shared 14 TB PostgreSQL primary, and every schema change is a company-wide event. Design the change-data-capture platform that ends that, and be honest about what gets harder.

Facts:
- The primary handles 22,000 write transactions/second at peak; 400 tables, of which 38 are in scope for CDC. The busiest table takes 9,000 inserts/second and 1,400 updates/second.
- Seven consumer classes with different needs: (a) a search indexer needing near-real-time (< 2 s) and tolerating duplicates; (b) an analytics warehouse loader tolerating 15 minutes but requiring exactly-once; (c) a cache invalidator needing < 500 ms and strict per-key ordering; (d) an audit archive requiring every intermediate value, never a collapsed one; (e) a fraud stream processor requiring transaction-level atomicity across three tables; (f) a partner webhook fan-out with at-least-once and a 24-hour replay window; (g) a materialized-view builder that must be able to rebuild from scratch in under 4 hours.
- Schema changes: roughly 30 per month, including column adds, column drops, type widenings, and two per year that are genuinely breaking.
- Retention of the change stream: 7 days hot, 90 days cold with replay capability.

Required:

1. Capture mechanism. Logical decoding versus trigger-based versus query-based polling. Choose, and quantify the write amplification and the replication-slot risk (specifically: what happens to the 14 TB primary when a consumer is down for 6 hours and the slot retains WAL; compute the WAL volume at 22k TPS and state your disk headroom).
2. Transport and topic design. Partitioning key, ordering guarantees, and how you satisfy BOTH consumer (c)'s strict per-key ordering and consumer (e)'s cross-table transaction atomicity, which pull in opposite directions. If you need two representations of the same data, say so and justify the duplication cost.
3. Delivery semantics. Explain exactly how consumer (b) gets exactly-once. Name the mechanism (idempotent writes, transactional offsets, dedup store) and its cost. Explain why (a) does not need it and what it saves.
4. Schema evolution. Define the compatibility policy per change type (add nullable, add non-null with default, drop, rename, widen int to bigint, narrow, change semantics without changing type). For each, state whether producers or consumers may deploy first, and what the registry enforces. Then handle the ugly one: a rename that a naive registry sees as a drop plus an add. Give the migration runbook.
5. Snapshot plus stream. How a new consumer bootstraps from a 14 TB table without blocking writes and without a gap or overlap at the seam. Describe the watermark protocol precisely enough to implement, and prove there is no lost or duplicated row at the boundary.
6. Capacity math: events/second, average serialized event size (state your format), MB/s, 7-day hot retention volume with replication factor, and consumer lag budget in bytes.
7. Failure modes, at least eight, including: a consumer that commits offsets it did not process, a primary failover that rewinds the LSN, an out-of-order delivery to the cache invalidator, a schema registry outage, a TOASTed column not present in the change event, and a 40-million-row single transaction from a batch job.
8. Rejected alternatives with the disqualifying detail: dual writes from application code, application-level outbox with a poller, read replicas for everyone, and a nightly bulk diff.

prompts.title: Edge session revocation in two seconds
prompts.text:
We terminate TLS at 190 points of presence and validate sessions there. Legal has now committed us to a hard requirement: when a session is revoked (logout-everywhere, password change, admin ban, or fraud signal) every PoP must stop honouring it within 2 seconds, worldwide. Currently we use 15-minute JWTs and our answer is 'wait 15 minutes'. That is no longer acceptable. Design the replacement.

Context:
- 240 million monthly active users, 41 million sessions active at any instant, 3.1 million session validations/second at the edge.
- The edge validation must add under 1.2 ms p99 and must work when the PoP is isolated from all origin datacenters (this happens: median 3 isolation events/month, median duration 90 seconds, worst observed 47 minutes).
- Revocation events: 26,000/day baseline, but a credential-stuffing response can produce 4 million revocations in 10 minutes.
- PoP hardware: 12 GiB of RAM available per PoP for this subsystem. Small PoPs have 3 servers, large ones 60.
- A false accept (honouring a revoked session) is a security incident. A false reject (rejecting a valid session) at a rate above 1 in 100,000 is a product incident.

Answer:

1. The token format. Stateless, stateful, or hybrid. If stateless, how revocation is possible at all; if stateful, how you meet 1.2 ms p99 at the edge without an origin round trip. Give the exact bytes on the wire and the validation steps in order.
2. The revocation propagation channel. Push topology from origin to 190 PoPs, ordering, deduplication, and the mechanism by which a PoP knows it has NOT missed a revocation (this matters more than delivery speed; a PoP that silently misses one is the security incident). Design the gap-detection and catch-up protocol and bound the exposure window.
3. Data structure at the edge. You must represent up to 41 million potentially-revoked identifiers in 12 GiB with a false-accept probability of zero. Note that a Bloom filter has the WRONG error direction here; explain why, and design accordingly. Compute memory for your structure, and handle the 4-million-revocations-in-10-minutes burst: show the peak size and the eviction/expiry rule that keeps it bounded. Prove your expiry rule cannot expire an entry while a token bearing it is still otherwise valid.
4. Isolation. During a 47-minute PoP isolation, what happens to (a) new revocations, (b) sessions revoked before isolation, (c) new logins. Choose fail-open or fail-closed per case and defend each choice with the actual business consequence.
5. Capacity math: bytes per revocation record, propagation bandwidth to 190 PoPs at burst rate, memory per PoP at steady state and at burst, and validation CPU cost per request at 3.1 million/second.
6. Clock. Your scheme almost certainly depends on time. Quantify the effect of 5 seconds of clock skew at one PoP on both false accepts and false rejects, and mitigate.
7. Failure modes: a PoP that comes back after 47 minutes, a malformed revocation that crashes the ingest, a replay of an old revocation batch, a compromised PoP, an origin that emits revocations for every user by mistake, and memory pressure causing eviction of live entries.
8. Rejected alternatives, minimum five, with the disqualifying number: short-lived JWTs at 30 seconds, per-request origin introspection, CRL-style periodic full lists, a globally replicated key-value store at the edge, and mutual TLS with client certs.
9. Give the acceptance test that proves the 2-second requirement is met, including how you would measure it in production continuously.

prompts.title: Weighted intervals with recovery time
prompts.text:
Here is a scheduling problem that is not quite the textbook one. Solve it properly.

A single machine processes jobs. You are given n jobs; job i is a tuple (s_i, f_i, r_i, w_i) where s_i < f_i are integer start and finish times, r_i >= 0 is an integer RECOVERY time, and w_i > 0 is a real weight. The machine may run job i only over the exact interval [s_i, f_i) - jobs cannot be shifted. After finishing job i the machine is unusable during [f_i, f_i + r_i). Therefore a schedule is a subset S of jobs such that for any two jobs i, j in S with f_i <= s_j, we require s_j >= f_i + r_i; and no two chosen jobs may overlap in time at all.

Goal: choose S maximizing the total weight sum of w_i.

Requirements for your answer:

1. Give an algorithm running in O(n log n) time and O(n) space. Anything slower is a fail. State the sort key(s) explicitly.
2. Define your dynamic-programming state with complete precision, including what index it is over and what the base case is. Do not write 'dp[i] = best answer up to i' without saying what 'up to' means when recovery times can push a predecessor's effective end past another job's start.
3. Prove the recurrence correct. Specifically, prove the exchange/optimal-substructure lemma you rely on, and be careful: the naive claim 'the predecessor of job i in an optimal solution is the job with the largest f_j + r_j <= s_i' is FALSE as stated. Either repair it into a true statement and prove that, or show a 3-job counterexample and then give the correct formulation.
4. Explain exactly how you achieve O(log n) per job for the predecessor lookup, given that the search key is f_j + r_j and the array is sorted by f_j. Note that f_j + r_j is not necessarily monotone in f_j. This is the crux of the problem - do not gloss over it. If it forces a different data structure or a different sort order, say which and why.
5. Handle these edge cases explicitly and say what your algorithm returns for each: all r_i = 0 (should reduce to classic weighted interval scheduling); a job with s_i = f_i (zero duration) and r_i = 5; two jobs with identical (s, f) but different weights; r_i so large that choosing job i forbids everything after it.
6. Give the reconstruction procedure that outputs the actual set S, not just its weight, in O(n) additional time.
7. Trace your algorithm by hand on this instance and give the exact optimal weight and the chosen set:
   J1 = (0, 3, 2, 5), J2 = (2, 4, 0, 4), J3 = (4, 6, 1, 6), J4 = (5, 9, 0, 7), J5 = (6, 7, 4, 3), J6 = (7, 10, 0, 8), J7 = (9, 12, 0, 6).
   Show the dp table row by row.
8. Finally, state what changes if the machine may run TWO jobs concurrently (2 machines, each with its own recovery). Is your approach still polynomial? Give the complexity or prove hardness.

prompts.title: Heavy hitters over deletions
prompts.text:
Design a sketch for the following streaming problem and prove its guarantees.

A stream of updates arrives, each of the form (key, delta) where key is drawn from a universe of size U = 2^64 and delta is an integer in [-1, +1]. Let c_x denote the net count of key x after processing the whole stream; c_x may be negative in the middle of the stream but is guaranteed non-negative at the end. Let L = sum over x of c_x at the end of the stream (the final L1 norm). The stream length m may be up to 10^11 and you may make exactly one pass.

You must support, at any point after the stream ends:
- pointQuery(x): return an estimate of c_x.
- heavyHitters(phi): return a set H containing every key with c_x >= phi*L, and containing no key with c_x < (phi - eps)*L.

Target: space O((1/eps) * log(1/delta) * log U) machine words, update time O(log(1/delta)) per element, and failure probability at most delta for the guarantees you state.

Deliver the following, in order:

1. Why the classic Misra-Gries / Space-Saving counters do NOT work here. Give a concrete adversarial stream with deletions on which Misra-Gries produces an arbitrarily wrong answer, with the numbers worked out.
2. Your sketch. Specify the hash families required (state the independence you need - pairwise, 4-wise, or full - and where each is used), the array dimensions in terms of eps and delta, and the exact update and query procedures in pseudocode.
3. The error bound. State it precisely (additive in eps*L? in eps*L2? one-sided or two-sided?) and PROVE it. Your proof must include the expectation computation, the variance or Markov/Chebyshev step, and the median-of-estimators amplification. Do not skip the step where you justify why the estimator is unbiased under deletions - this is where the classic Count-Min analysis breaks and you must either switch estimators or restrict the guarantee.
4. The heavy-hitters retrieval. Storing all candidate keys is not allowed at 2^64 universe size. Give the hierarchical/dyadic-range construction that lets you recover the heavy keys in O((1/phi) * log U * (query cost)) time, prove that it finds every phi-heavy key, and compute the total space including the extra levels.
5. Concrete numbers: set eps = 0.001, delta = 0.01, U = 2^64. Compute the actual array dimensions, the total memory in megabytes assuming 8-byte counters, and the number of hash evaluations per update. Show the arithmetic.
6. Prove or disprove: 'with the guarantees above, the returned set H can be shown to have size at most 1/phi'. If it is false, give the true bound on |H| and the stream that achieves it.
7. Discuss what breaks if the final counts are allowed to be negative, and state the modified guarantee.

prompts.title: Orienting a mixed graph
prompts.text:
Mixed-graph orientation problem. Read carefully - the input is partly directed.

You are given a graph G on n vertices and m edges. Some edges are directed (an ordered pair) and some are undirected. You must assign a direction to every undirected edge so that the resulting fully-directed graph is strongly connected, or report that no such assignment exists.

What I want:

1. A correct characterization of feasibility. State the necessary and sufficient condition in terms of the structure of G, and prove BOTH directions. Your proof of sufficiency should be constructive (i.e. it should yield the algorithm). You will need the classical result about orienting undirected graphs, and you will need to say precisely how the presence of pre-directed edges changes it - do not just cite the theorem, prove the mixed version.
2. An algorithm running in O(n + m) time. Give it in enough detail to implement: the traversal, what you record at each vertex, and the rule that decides each undirected edge's direction. If you use a DFS with lowpoint values, define lowpoint exactly for the mixed setting, because the standard definition assumes undirected edges.
3. A correctness proof for the algorithm that is separate from the characterization proof: show that if the condition holds, the orientation your algorithm outputs really is strongly connected. An argument by 'every vertex can reach the root and the root can reach every vertex' is acceptable only if you prove both halves.
4. The following instance. Vertices 1..8. Directed edges: 1->2, 3->4, 6->5, 8->7. Undirected edges: {2,3}, {4,1}, {2,5}, {5,6}, {6,7}, {7,8}, {8,2}, {4,6}. Decide feasibility, and if feasible output a concrete orientation of all eight undirected edges and verify strong connectivity by exhibiting, for each vertex, a path to vertex 1 and from vertex 1.
5. A second instance that is INFEASIBLE, constructed by you, with at least 6 vertices and at least 2 pre-directed edges, plus the proof of infeasibility using your characterization.
6. Now a variant: each undirected edge e has two costs, cost_forward(e) and cost_backward(e), and you want a strongly connected orientation of minimum total cost. Is this still polynomial? Either give a polynomial algorithm with its complexity, or give a reduction from a known NP-hard problem with the gadget spelled out. Be decisive - a hedged answer scores zero.
7. State what your algorithm does on these degenerate inputs: n = 1 with no edges; a graph with a self-loop; parallel edges between the same pair, one directed and one undirected; a graph that is already fully directed.

prompts.title: Constant-time min deque
prompts.text:
Build me a data structure and prove its amortized bound rigorously.

Required operations, all on a sequence of comparable elements:
- pushFront(x), pushBack(x)
- popFront(), popBack()
- min(): return the minimum of all elements currently stored, without removing it

Target: every operation must be O(1) AMORTIZED, with O(n) space. A solution that gives O(log n) for min, or O(1) only for a single-ended queue, does not count. You may not use a balanced BST or a heap.

Write up:

1. The construction. The well-known two-stack trick gives an O(1)-amortized min-QUEUE. Explain why the straightforward extension to a deque breaks: give the exact operation sequence of length 2k that forces Theta(k) work per operation under the naive rebalance rule (move everything from the non-empty stack to the empty one). Compute the total cost of that sequence.
2. The fix. Describe the rebalancing policy that repairs it - specifically, what you do when one side runs empty (hint: it involves splitting rather than transferring wholesale, and the split ratio matters). State the policy as an explicit rule with the constant in it.
3. The amortized proof. Define a potential function Phi over the structure's state. Show Phi >= 0 always, Phi(initial) = 0, and compute the amortized cost of each of the five operations as actual cost + Delta(Phi). You must show the arithmetic for the expensive rebalance case and demonstrate that Delta(Phi) cancels the linear term. State the resulting constant.
4. Prove that the adversarial sequence you gave in part 1 now costs O(1) per operation under the fixed policy, by running your potential argument on it.
5. Auxiliary min tracking. Explain how each stack maintains its own running minimum in O(1), and why min() is then just a comparison of at most two values. Handle the case where one side is empty.
6. Extend to a second query: kthSmallest is NOT required, but rangeMinFront(k) - the minimum of the first k elements from the front - IS. Give the best complexity you can achieve for it without breaking the O(1) amortized bounds of the other five operations, and justify it. If you believe O(1) is impossible for rangeMinFront, argue why (an information-theoretic or cell-probe style argument is welcome; a hand-wave is not).
7. Worked trace. Start empty. Execute: pushBack(5), pushBack(3), pushFront(9), pushBack(7), min(), popFront(), min(), popBack(), popFront(), pushFront(2), pushBack(4), min(), popBack(), min(). At every step show the contents of both internal stacks, their running minima, the value of Phi, the actual cost, and the amortized cost. The trace must be internally consistent with the policy you defined in part 2.
8. State whether your bounds can be made worst-case O(1) rather than amortized, and sketch how (incremental rebuilding) or explain the obstacle.

prompts.title: K facilities on a tree
prompts.text:
Tree facility location with a tight complexity requirement.

Input: a tree T with n vertices, each edge e having a positive integer length len(e), each vertex v having a non-negative integer demand d(v), and an integer k with 1 <= k <= n. Choose a set F of exactly k vertices ('facilities'). The cost of a choice is sum over all vertices v of d(v) * dist(v, F), where dist(v, F) is the tree distance from v to the nearest vertex in F. Minimize the cost.

Requirements:

1. Give an exact algorithm running in O(n * k) time. Note the trap: the obvious tree-knapsack DP where you combine children with a convolution appears to cost O(n * k^2). You must present the standard sizing argument that the total convolution work over the whole tree is actually O(n * k), and you must PROVE it - a proof by 'it is well known' is rejected. The proof should count, for each pair of vertices, how many times that pair is charged, and conclude with the O(n*k) bound (or O(n^2) when k >= n, whichever is smaller). State the bound precisely.
2. Define the DP state. You will need more than 'best cost for subtree of v using j facilities', because the cost of a vertex in v's subtree may be paid by a facility OUTSIDE the subtree. Introduce the extra dimension (the distance to the nearest open facility on the path to the root, or the 'closest facility not yet chosen' trick), state its domain, and explain how you keep the state space from blowing up to O(n^2 k). If your solution requires the classic 'guess the distance to the nearest ancestor facility' technique, bound the number of distinct useful distances and justify the bound.
3. Prove the recurrence correct via an optimal-substructure lemma. State the lemma formally and prove it, including the case where the optimal solution assigns a vertex in v's subtree to a facility outside it.
4. Root choice. Explain whether the answer depends on which vertex you root at, and prove your claim.
5. Work this instance completely. Tree edges (u, v, len): (1,2,4), (1,3,2), (3,4,3), (3,5,1), (5,6,6), (2,7,5), (2,8,2). Demands: d(1)=3, d(2)=1, d(3)=4, d(4)=2, d(5)=7, d(6)=1, d(7)=5, d(8)=2. Compute the optimal cost and the optimal facility set for k = 1, k = 2, and k = 3. Show enough of the DP to make the answers checkable, and sanity-check k=1 by brute force over all 8 vertices (show the 8 totals).
6. Monotonicity. Prove or disprove: the optimal cost is non-increasing in k, and the optimal facility set for k+1 always contains the optimal set for k. One of these is true and one is false - identify which, prove the true one, and give a small counterexample for the false one (your counterexample must be a tree, and you must show both optimal sets).
7. State the complexity of your final algorithm in both time and space, and give the space-reduction trick if your DP naively stores O(n*k) integers per vertex.

prompts.title: Longest common substring of k strings
prompts.text:
Given m strings S_1, ..., S_m over an alphabet of size sigma <= 256, with total length N = sum |S_i| up to 5 * 10^6, and an integer k with 2 <= k <= m: find the longest string that occurs as a substring of AT LEAST k of the m strings. If several are tied for longest, return the lexicographically smallest. If no string of length >= 1 qualifies, say so.

Hard requirements:

1. Total running time O(N log N) or better; O(N * m) is explicitly rejected, and so is any solution whose complexity multiplies N by k or by sigma in a way that matters at N = 5*10^6, m = 10^5.
2. Memory O(N) words.

Produce:

1. Your chosen structure - generalized suffix automaton, suffix array of the concatenation with separators, or suffix tree - and a justification of the choice under the memory bound. If you concatenate with separators, explain what goes wrong if you use a single repeated separator character and how you avoid it without inflating the alphabet to m symbols (this detail matters; be specific).
2. The counting subproblem. For each candidate substring you need 'how many DISTINCT input strings contain it', not 'how many occurrences'. Explain precisely how you compute that, and why the naive per-node set union is too slow. Give the technique you use (small-to-large merging, bitset over m, DSU on tree, or an offline sweep) and its exact complexity. If you use small-to-large, prove the O(N log N) bound; if you use a different technique, prove its bound.
3. The lexicographic tie-break. Explain how you find the lexicographically smallest among all longest qualifying substrings without enumerating them all. If your primary structure does not make this easy, say so and give the extra step.
4. Prove correctness: that every substring your method considers is genuinely a substring of the reported number of strings, and that no longer qualifying substring is missed. Handle the subtlety that a substring occurring twice in the same S_i must be counted once.
5. Edge cases with stated outputs: k = m and the strings share nothing; k = 2 and two identical strings; a string of length 1; an input containing an empty string; all m strings equal.
6. Solve this instance by hand and show your work: S_1 = 'abcabdac', S_2 = 'zbcabqq', S_3 = 'bcabt', S_4 = 'xxbcaby', S_5 = 'cabbca', with k = 4. Give the answer and demonstrate why nothing longer qualifies by exhibiting, for each candidate one character longer, at least two strings that lack it.
7. Now change the problem: 'at least k of the m strings' becomes 'at least k CONSECUTIVE strings in the given order'. Does your approach still work? Give the modified algorithm and complexity, or explain what breaks.

prompts.title: Depth-bounded interval selection
prompts.text:
Consider this interval selection variant, which is NOT the standard one.

You are given n closed intervals [a_i, b_i] with integer endpoints, and an integer k >= 1. Select a subset S of the intervals maximizing |S|, subject to: for every point p on the real line, the number of intervals in S that contain p is at most k. (For k = 1 this is ordinary interval scheduling; for k >= 2 it is not.)

Deliver:

1. An O(n log n) algorithm. State the sort order and the auxiliary structure. If you use a greedy, state the greedy rule in one sentence, unambiguously.
2. A proof of optimality. An exchange argument is expected: assume an optimal solution OPT differs from the greedy solution G at the first decision point, and transform OPT into a solution that agrees with G without decreasing its size and without violating the depth-k constraint. The depth constraint makes the swap non-trivial - the interval you remove from OPT may not be removable without cascading. Handle that case explicitly; a proof that only works for k = 1 will be marked wrong.
3. A counterexample gallery. For each of the following plausible greedy rules, either prove it optimal or give a concrete counterexample instance (with k, the intervals, the greedy's answer, and the true optimum):
   (a) sort by left endpoint ascending, take if depth allows;
   (b) sort by length ascending, take if depth allows;
   (c) sort by right endpoint ascending, take if depth allows;
   (d) sort by right endpoint ascending, but when the depth constraint blocks an interval, evict the already-selected interval with the largest right endpoint if that helps.
   At least two of these are wrong. Your counterexamples must be minimal-ish (at most 8 intervals) and fully worked.
4. Data structure detail. Checking 'does adding [a,b] exceed depth k anywhere in [a,b]' naively is O(n) per interval. Give the structure that makes it O(log n) - specify whether you use a max-segment-tree with lazy range add and a range-max query, a BIT over a difference array, or a sweep with a multiset - and state exactly what is stored and what is queried.
5. Now weight the intervals: interval i has weight w_i > 0 and you want maximum total weight under the same depth-k constraint. Prove that the greedy from part 1 is NOT optimal by giving a counterexample. Then give a polynomial algorithm for the weighted version, identify the underlying combinatorial structure (min-cost flow on an interval graph, an LP whose constraint matrix is an interval matrix and therefore totally unimodular, or a DP), and state its complexity. If you invoke total unimodularity you must say which matrix and why it is TU.
6. Work this instance for k = 2: [1,4], [2,6], [3,5], [5,9], [6,8], [7,12], [8,10], [11,13], [1,13], [4,7]. Give the maximum |S|, the actual set, and the depth profile of your solution at every integer point 1..13 to prove feasibility. Then compute the optimum for k = 1 and k = 3 on the same instance.

prompts.title: Offline dynamic connectivity
prompts.text:
Implement-and-prove task: offline dynamic connectivity.

You are given n vertices and a sequence of q operations, all known in advance (offline):
- ADD u v: insert an undirected edge (u,v); the same pair may be inserted multiple times
- DEL u v: delete one copy of an existing edge (u,v)
- ASK u v: report whether u and v are currently in the same connected component
- SIZE u: report the size of the component containing u

Required complexity: O((n + q) log q * alpha(n)) time and O(n + q) space, where alpha is the inverse Ackermann function. Amortization across the whole run is allowed; per-operation worst case is not required. Solutions using link-cut trees or Euler-tour trees are acceptable ONLY if you also give the offline segment-tree solution and compare, because the offline structure is the point of the exercise.

Write:

1. The edge-lifetime decomposition. Explain how each edge insertion/deletion pair becomes a half-open interval of operation indices, how you handle an edge inserted but never deleted, and how you handle multiple simultaneous copies of the same edge. Then explain the segment tree over the time axis and prove that each edge interval decomposes into at most 2*log(q) nodes.
2. The DSU with rollback. Explain why path compression must be dropped, which heuristic you keep (union by size or by rank), and prove the resulting O(log n) worst-case find. Then define the rollback stack precisely: what you push on a union, what you pop, and why a no-op union must still push something. That last detail is the classic bug - address it explicitly.
3. The traversal. Give the recursive procedure over the segment tree, stating the invariant that holds when the recursion is at node X ('the DSU currently reflects exactly the edges alive throughout X's whole time range'). Prove that the invariant is preserved by the recursion.
4. Prove the total complexity, counting the number of union operations performed across the entire traversal and the cost of each.
5. Answering SIZE u requires component sizes to be correct at leaf time. Show that union-by-size gives this for free and that rollback restores it exactly.
6. Now the hard part. Explain what specifically breaks if you try to use this structure for BIPARTITENESS queries ('is the current graph bipartite?') and then FIX it: give the DSU-with-parity variant, the extra field, the union rule, the rollback rule, and the odd-cycle detection. Prove your parity invariant.
7. Then explain why this same offline framework CANNOT be adapted to answer 'is there a directed path from u to v' under directed edge insertions and deletions, at least not by the same rollback trick. Identify the exact algebraic property that DSU-with-rollback relies on and that directed reachability lacks.
8. Trace: n = 6, operations: ADD 1 2, ADD 2 3, ASK 1 3, ADD 4 5, DEL 2 3, ASK 1 3, ADD 3 4, ADD 1 3, ASK 1 5, SIZE 1, DEL 1 3, ASK 1 5, SIZE 4. Give the answer to every ASK and SIZE, and show the segment-tree node assignment for each edge interval.

prompts.title: Assignment with forbidden pairs
prompts.text:
A combinatorial feasibility question, plus an algorithm, plus a proof.

There are p tasks and q workers. Worker j has capacity c_j >= 1 (it can be assigned up to c_j tasks). Task i requires exactly one worker and has a set A_i of workers that are able to perform it. Additionally there is a set of FORBIDDEN PAIRS: a list of pairs of tasks {i, i'} that must not be assigned to the same worker (they conflict - think of two tasks that would deadlock if colocated).

Part A - the version WITHOUT forbidden pairs.
1. State the exact necessary and sufficient condition for a feasible assignment to exist, generalizing Hall's theorem to the capacitated case. Prove both directions. Your proof of sufficiency may go via flows, but then you must justify integrality of the maximum flow rather than assuming it.
2. Give an algorithm and its complexity in terms of p, q, and E = sum |A_i|. State the flow network precisely: nodes, arcs, capacities, source, sink. Compute the value of a maximum flow that corresponds to a feasible assignment.
3. When infeasible, produce a certificate: a set of tasks whose combined worker capacity is insufficient. Prove your certificate extraction from a min cut is correct.

Part B - the version WITH forbidden pairs.
4. Prove that the general problem with arbitrary forbidden pairs is NP-complete. Give the reduction from a specific NP-complete problem, define the gadget precisely, and prove both directions of the reduction (a valid assignment implies a valid solution to the source instance, and conversely). Be careful to also argue membership in NP.
5. Now restrict: suppose the conflict graph (vertices = tasks, edges = forbidden pairs) is a disjoint union of cliques, and every worker has capacity 1. Show that the problem becomes polynomial and give the algorithm and complexity.
6. Restrict differently: the conflict graph is a perfect matching (each task conflicts with at most one other task) and capacities are arbitrary. Is this polynomial? Decide and justify. If yes, give the algorithm; if no, give the reduction.

Part C - a concrete instance.
7. Tasks T1..T7, workers W1..W4 with capacities c(W1)=2, c(W2)=2, c(W3)=1, c(W4)=3.
   A(T1) = {W1, W2}, A(T2) = {W1}, A(T3) = {W2, W3}, A(T4) = {W1, W2, W4}, A(T5) = {W3, W4}, A(T6) = {W4}, A(T7) = {W2, W4}.
   Forbidden pairs: {T1, T4}, {T5, T6}, {T3, T7}.
   Determine whether a feasible assignment exists. If yes, give one explicitly and verify every capacity and every forbidden pair. If no, prove infeasibility with a counting argument that names the specific set of tasks and the specific capacity shortfall.
8. Then change c(W4) from 3 to 2 and redo the analysis. State whether the answer changes and why.

prompts.title: Streaming triangle count estimator
prompts.text:
Streaming graph estimation, with a full probabilistic analysis.

Edges of a simple undirected graph G = (V, E) arrive one at a time in adversarial order; |V| = n is known in advance, |E| = m is not. One pass, sublinear space. Let T be the number of triangles in G. You may assume T >= T_min for a known threshold T_min (state where you need this assumption).

Goal: output an estimate T_hat with Pr[ |T_hat - T| > eps * T ] <= delta.

Write the following:

1. The single-estimator scheme. Describe an unbiased one-shot estimator that uses O(1) words of space: sample a uniformly random edge from the stream using reservoir sampling, then sample a second structure, then test. Give the exact sampling procedure and the exact output value of the estimator (including the scaling factor). Prove E[X] = T for your estimator X. The proof must compute the probability that a specific triangle is 'detected' and show the scaling cancels it.
2. Variance. Compute or bound Var[X], expressing it in terms of m, T, and any other graph parameter you need (you will probably need the number of paths of length 2, or the maximum number of triangles sharing an edge - introduce it explicitly and name it). Show the algebra.
3. Amplification. Combine k independent copies by averaging, then take a median of l such averages. Derive the values of k and l needed for the (eps, delta) guarantee. State the total space in words as a function of eps, delta, n, m, T, and the parameter from step 2. This is where T_min enters - explain how.
4. Order matters. Your reservoir sampling of the 'second' element must be uniform over edges arriving AFTER the first sample, or uniform over all edges - pick one and explain why the other choice breaks the unbiasedness proof. Give the corrected estimator for whichever choice you make.
5. Concrete numbers. n = 10^6, m = 5*10^7, T = 10^8, maximum triangles per edge = 500, eps = 0.1, delta = 0.05. Compute k, l, and the total memory in megabytes assuming 8 bytes per word and 3 words per estimator. Show the arithmetic.
6. A lower bound discussion. Argue informally but concretely why no one-pass algorithm can distinguish T = 0 from T = 1 in o(n^2) space for general graphs, sketching a reduction from set-disjointness in communication complexity. State the reduction's two players, their inputs, and what a small-space streaming algorithm would imply.
7. Prove or disprove this claim: 'if the graph has no two triangles sharing an edge, then the variance bound in step 2 simplifies enough that O(m / (eps^2 * T)) space suffices with no dependence on n'. Give the derivation either way.
8. Finally, adapt the estimator to a stream that also contains edge DELETIONS (turnstile model). State clearly whether your reservoir-based approach survives, and if not, name the alternative primitive you would use and the space it costs.

prompts.title: Five proofs, some broken
prompts.text:
Below are five claimed theorems, each with a claimed proof. For EACH item you must produce four things:
(i) is the STATEMENT true or false;
(ii) is the PROOF valid;
(iii) if the proof is invalid, quote the first sentence that is wrong or unjustified and explain precisely what is wrong with it (not a vague 'this step is hand-wavy');
(iv) if the statement is true but the proof is broken, supply a correct proof; if the statement is false, supply a concrete minimal counterexample and verify it against the statement.

Do not skip items and do not merge them. Four of these are interesting; one is fine.

--- ITEM A ---
Statement: Every finite simple graph in which every vertex has degree at least 2 contains a cycle.
Proof: We argue by induction on the number of vertices n. For the base case n = 3, the only simple graph on three vertices in which every vertex has degree at least 2 is the triangle, which contains a cycle. Now suppose the claim holds for all such graphs on n vertices, and let G be a simple graph on n+1 vertices in which every vertex has degree at least 2. Pick any vertex v and delete it, obtaining G - v, a simple graph on n vertices in which every vertex still has degree at least 2. By the induction hypothesis, G - v contains a cycle C. Since G - v is a subgraph of G, C is also a cycle of G. This completes the induction.

--- ITEM B ---
Statement: Let F be defined by F(1) = 1, F(2) = 1, and F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2) for n >= 3. Then F(n) <= 1.7^n for every n >= 1.
Proof: We use strong induction. Base case: n = 1, and F(1) = 1 <= 1.7 = 1.7^1. For the inductive step, let n >= 2 and suppose F(k) <= 1.7^k for all k < n. Then F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2) <= 1.7^(n-1) + 1.7^(n-2) = 1.7^(n-2) * (1.7 + 1) = 2.7 * 1.7^(n-2). Since 1.7^2 = 2.89 >= 2.7, we get 2.7 * 1.7^(n-2) <= 1.7^2 * 1.7^(n-2) = 1.7^n. Hence F(n) <= 1.7^n, completing the induction.

--- ITEM C ---
Statement: Every simple graph with n vertices and exactly n - 1 edges is a tree.
Proof: It is standard that every tree on n vertices has exactly n - 1 edges, so we prove the converse. Let G have n vertices and n - 1 edges. Suppose for contradiction that G contains a cycle C, and let e be any edge of C. Removing e from G leaves the graph connected, because any path that used e can be rerouted the other way around C. So G - e is a connected graph on n vertices with n - 2 edges. But a connected graph on n vertices has at least n - 1 edges, a contradiction. Therefore G is acyclic. An acyclic graph on n vertices with n - 1 edges is a tree, so G is a tree.

--- ITEM D ---
Statement: For every integer n >= 0, 6 divides n^3 - n.
Proof: Induction on n. Base case n = 0: 0^3 - 0 = 0, and 6 divides 0. Inductive step: assume 6 divides n^3 - n. Then (n+1)^3 - (n+1) = n^3 + 3n^2 + 3n + 1 - n - 1 = (n^3 - n) + 3n^2 + 3n = (n^3 - n) + 3n(n+1). The first term is divisible by 6 by the induction hypothesis. For the second, n and n+1 are consecutive integers, so one of them is even, hence n(n+1) is even, hence 3n(n+1) is divisible by 6. A sum of two multiples of 6 is a multiple of 6, so 6 divides (n+1)^3 - (n+1).

--- ITEM E ---
Statement: Every integer n >= 2 can be written as a product of (one or more) primes.
Proof: We induct on n. Base case: n = 2 is prime, and a single prime is a product of primes. Inductive step: suppose n >= 2 can be written as a product of primes; we show n + 1 can be. If n + 1 is prime we are done. Otherwise n + 1 is composite, so n + 1 = a * b with 1 < a < n + 1 and 1 < b < n + 1. By the induction hypothesis, a and b are each products of primes, so their product n + 1 is a product of primes. This completes the induction.

After finishing all five items, answer this closing question: exactly one of the five broken proofs can be repaired by changing at most two words or numbers, without adding any new argument. Identify which one, give the edit, and explain why the other broken proofs need a genuinely different argument rather than a patch.

prompts.title: Binary search invariant audit
prompts.text:
Four candidate implementations of lower_bound are given below. Each is supposed to return, for a non-decreasing array a of length n and a value x, the smallest index i in [0, n] such that a[i] >= x (returning n if no such element exists). Arrays are 0-indexed. Integer division truncates toward zero and all values fit in the integer type, so overflow is not the issue here.

VARIANT 1
  lo = 0; hi = n
  while lo < hi:
      mid = (lo + hi) // 2
      if a[mid] < x: lo = mid
      else: hi = mid
  return lo

VARIANT 2
  lo = 0; hi = n
  while lo < hi:
      mid = (lo + hi) // 2
      if a[mid] < x: lo = mid + 1
      else: hi = mid
  return lo

VARIANT 3
  lo = 0; hi = n - 1
  while lo <= hi:
      mid = (lo + hi) // 2
      if a[mid] < x: lo = mid + 1
      else: hi = mid - 1
  return lo

VARIANT 4
  lo = -1; hi = n
  while hi - lo > 1:
      mid = (lo + hi) // 2
      if a[mid] < x: lo = mid
      else: hi = mid
  return hi

For each variant, do all of the following, keeping the four analyses separate:

1. State the loop invariant as a precise logical formula over lo, hi, a, x, and n. It must be strong enough that the invariant together with the negated loop condition implies the postcondition. Do not write an English paraphrase; write the formula, then explain it in one sentence.
2. Prove that the invariant holds on entry to the loop, including for n = 0.
3. Prove that each iteration preserves the invariant, considering both branches. If it does not, say exactly which branch breaks it and give a two-element array plus a value of x that exhibits the break.
4. Prove termination by exhibiting a variant function (a non-negative integer quantity that strictly decreases every iteration) or prove that no such function exists.
5. Prove that invariant + negated loop guard implies the specification, or show where the implication fails.
6. Give the exact verdict: CORRECT, INCORRECT-WRONG-ANSWER, or INCORRECT-NONTERMINATING. If incorrect, give the smallest counterexample by array length, with the array, the value of x, the expected answer, and the actual behaviour (the returned value, or the sequence of (lo, hi, mid) triples that repeats forever).

Then answer these cross-cutting questions:

A. Variant 4 uses mid = (lo + hi) // 2 with lo starting at -1. In a language where integer division truncates toward zero rather than flooring, does variant 4 still terminate and still compute the right answer? Work through lo = -1, hi = 0 explicitly and state what happens under each division convention.
B. One of the variants computes the correct answer but has a subtly different invariant than you might expect, because its search space is a half-open interval on one side and an open interval on the other. Identify it and state the interval semantics explicitly.
C. For the variant(s) you judged correct, prove the exact iteration count as a function of n, and state whether it is ceil(log2(n+1)) or floor(log2(n)) + 1 or something else. Verify your formula against n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9 by listing the counts.
D. Modify the correct variant minimally to compute upper_bound (the smallest index i with a[i] > x). Give the diff and re-state the invariant with the change highlighted.

prompts.title: Disproving a Hamiltonicity claim
prompts.text:
A colleague has written the following in a design note, and I need it either confirmed or demolished rigorously.

CLAIM: 'Every 2-connected simple graph contains a Hamiltonian cycle.'

His argument: 'A graph is 2-connected exactly when it has no cut vertex, so you can never get stranded: from any vertex there are at least two internally disjoint routes to any other vertex. Start at any vertex and walk, always leaving by an unused edge. Because there is no cut vertex, deleting the vertex you are currently standing on cannot disconnect the rest of the graph, so the remaining unvisited vertices are always mutually reachable and you can never paint yourself into a corner. Continue until every vertex is visited; the two-connectivity guarantees an edge back to the start, closing the cycle.'

Do the following, in order:

1. Decide whether the CLAIM is true or false. Be unambiguous.
2. If false, give a counterexample. Give it as an explicit vertex set and edge list, prove it is 2-connected (by exhibiting, for every vertex, that its deletion leaves a connected graph, or by a cleaner argument), and prove it has no Hamiltonian cycle. The non-Hamiltonicity proof must be a proof, not an appeal to 'I tried and failed' - use a counting or bipartition argument.
3. Prove that your counterexample is MINIMUM in the number of vertices among all 2-connected non-Hamiltonian simple graphs. That is, show that every 2-connected simple graph on fewer vertices than yours is Hamiltonian. You may organize this by vertex count and use the fact that 2-connectedness forces minimum degree at least 2; be exhaustive about the small cases rather than asserting them.
4. Identify the exact sentence in your colleague's argument that is unjustified, and explain the flaw in terms of what the greedy walk actually needs (it needs more than 'the unvisited part stays connected'). Construct a small graph and a specific partial walk on it where his procedure is stuck with unvisited vertices remaining, and present the walk step by step.
5. Now state and prove a correct sufficient condition. Prove ORE'S THEOREM: if G is a simple graph on n >= 3 vertices and deg(u) + deg(v) >= n for every pair of non-adjacent vertices u, v, then G is Hamiltonian. Give the full proof (the standard route is: assume a maximally non-Hamiltonian counterexample, take a Hamiltonian path, and derive a contradiction by a rotation/crossing argument on the neighbourhoods of the path endpoints). Do not cite it; prove it.
6. Check your counterexample from step 2 against Ore's condition: name a specific non-adjacent pair whose degree sum is less than n, and give the numbers.
7. Finally, decide these two follow-up statements, proving or refuting each:
   (a) 'Every 3-connected planar graph is Hamiltonian.'
   (b) 'Every 2-connected graph has a cycle through any two specified vertices.'
   One of them is a real theorem with a well-known name and one is refutable; identify which is which. For the refutable one give a counterexample; for the true one, state the theorem's name and give a proof sketch of the key lemma it rests on.

prompts.title: Linearizability of six histories
prompts.text:
You are auditing concurrent object histories. Time is given as integer ticks; an operation is written as PROCESS: op(args) -> result [invocation_tick, response_tick]. All histories below are complete (every invocation has a matching response). Objects start in the state noted.

HISTORY H1 - object: FIFO queue, initially empty
  P: enq(x) -> ok   [1, 5]
  Q: enq(y) -> ok   [2, 6]
  P: deq() -> y     [7, 9]
  Q: deq() -> x     [8, 10]

HISTORY H2 - object: FIFO queue, initially empty
  P: enq(x) -> ok   [1, 2]
  Q: enq(y) -> ok   [3, 4]
  R: deq() -> y     [5, 6]
  R: deq() -> x     [7, 8]

HISTORY H3 - object: read/write register, initial value 0
  P: write(1) -> ok [1, 2]
  Q: read() -> 0    [3, 4]

HISTORY H4 - object: read/write register, initial value 0
  P: write(1) -> ok [1, 10]
  Q: read() -> 1    [2, 3]
  R: read() -> 0    [4, 5]

HISTORY H5 - object: read/write register, initial value 0
  P: write(1) -> ok [1, 4]
  Q: write(2) -> ok [2, 6]
  R: read() -> 1    [7, 8]
  S: read() -> 2    [9, 10]

HISTORY H6 - object: compare-and-swap register, initial value 0
  P: cas(0, 1) -> true   [1, 6]
  Q: cas(0, 2) -> false  [2, 4]
  R: read() -> 0         [3, 5]
  S: read() -> 1         [7, 8]

For every history H1 through H6 answer, with proof:

1. Is it LINEARIZABLE? If yes, exhibit a witness: a total order on the operations that (a) is a legal sequential history for the object type, and (b) respects real-time precedence (if op1's response tick is strictly less than op2's invocation tick, op1 precedes op2 in the order). Give the linearization POINT for each operation as a tick inside its interval, and verify each point lies in its interval. If no, give a proof of impossibility: identify a specific set of operations whose required orderings form a cycle, and exhibit the cycle explicitly with the reason for each edge.
2. Is it SEQUENTIALLY CONSISTENT? Same standard of evidence. Note that sequential consistency drops the real-time requirement but keeps per-process program order.
3. Where the two answers differ, say in one sentence which requirement did the work.

Then the theory part:

4. Prove that linearizability is a LOCAL (composable) property: if every object's projection of a history is linearizable, the whole history is linearizable. Give the actual proof - the standard route constructs a partial order from the per-object linearizations plus real-time order and shows it is acyclic. The acyclicity argument is the whole content; do it carefully.
5. Prove that sequential consistency is NOT local by constructing a two-object history on two processes where each object's projection is sequentially consistent but the combined history is not. Give the history in the same notation as above and prove both halves.
6. H6 contains a subtlety: Q's cas(0,2) returns false while R concurrently reads 0. Explain why this is not automatically a contradiction, and state the precise condition on linearization points that makes it consistent or inconsistent. Then give the verdict for H6 with the reasoning laid out.
7. Finally, modify H4 by changing exactly one tick number so that it becomes linearizable, state which number you changed, and give the witness order. Prove that changing any single tick in H2 cannot make it linearizable.

prompts.title: Pigeonhole battery with a trap
prompts.text:
Six statements follow. Some are true and some are false. For every one: decide, then either give a complete proof or give an explicit counterexample together with a verification. Where a statement is true and tight, also prove the tightness claim attached to it. Show your reasoning; a bare verdict earns nothing.

S1. For every integer n >= 1: among any n + 1 distinct integers chosen from {1, 2, ..., 2n}, there exist two, a and b, such that a divides b.
   Tightness to prove or refute: there exists a choice of n distinct integers from {1, ..., 2n} in which no element divides another.

S2. For every integer n >= 1: among any n + 1 distinct integers chosen from {1, 2, ..., 2n}, there exist two that are coprime.

S3. For every integer n >= 1: among any n + 1 distinct integers chosen from {1, 2, ..., 2n}, there exist two whose difference is exactly n.

S4. For every integer n >= 2: among any n + 1 distinct integers chosen from {1, 2, ..., 2n}, there exist three distinct elements a, b, c with a + b = c.

S5. Among any 5 points placed in a closed unit square (side length 1), some two of them are at Euclidean distance at most 0.7.
   And separately: among any 5 points placed in a closed unit square, some two are at distance at most sqrt(2)/2. Decide BOTH, since they are not the same statement, and if one is true and one is false explain exactly where the boundary lies and why the constant matters.

S6. Given any 10 distinct two-digit positive integers (that is, from {10, 11, ..., 99}), there exist two disjoint non-empty subsets of them with the same sum.

Guidance on what a complete answer looks like:
- For S1, the standard proof writes each chosen integer as 2^k * m with m odd and pigeonholes on m. Say how many possible values m has and why that is the pigeonhole count. Then prove the divisibility conclusion actually follows (two numbers with the same odd part do satisfy the divisibility relation - show it).
- For any statement you judge FALSE, your counterexample must name a specific n (or specific points/numbers), list the elements, and verify the failure exhaustively or by a short argument covering all pairs/triples.
- For S5, the correct threshold is a specific constant. Give the configuration that shows tightness and compute its minimum pairwise distance exactly, in surd form and to four decimal places. Then state which of the two versions of S5 is false and why the difference between 0.7 and sqrt(2)/2 is decisive, quoting the numeric comparison.
- For S6, count the number of non-empty subsets and bound the number of achievable sums; show the strict inequality that makes pigeonhole apply, and then explain the extra step needed to turn 'two subsets with equal sum' into 'two DISJOINT subsets with equal sum'. That extra step is the part most people omit; do not omit it.

Finally: exactly one of S1-S6 is false. State which, and for each of the other five, give a one-line summary of the pigeonhole structure used (what are the pigeons, what are the holes, and what is the count).

prompts.title: On-call roster constraint puzzle
prompts.text:
Solve this constraint satisfaction problem and prove that your solution is the only one.

Five engineers - Ada, Bo, Cy, Di, Ed - each took exactly one on-call shift last week, one per weekday (Monday through Friday, in that order). Each shift covered exactly one service (Auth, Billing, Ledger, Media, Search), was served out of exactly one region (af, ap, eu, sa, us), and generated exactly one of the page counts 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Every engineer, day, service, region and page count is used exactly once. Deduce the complete assignment.

Clues:
1. Ed's shift produced more pages than any other shift that week.
2. Ada's shift was on an earlier weekday than Cy's, and Cy's was on an earlier weekday than Ed's.
3. The Ledger shift was on the weekday immediately after the Search shift.
4. Bo did not cover Auth and did not cover Billing.
5. The shift served out of the eu region produced exactly 6 pages.
6. Di was on call on Friday.
7. The Media shift was served out of the af region.
8. Tuesday's shift produced fewer pages than every other shift that week.
9. The us-region shift was on the weekday immediately after the eu-region shift.
10. Ed covered Search.
11. The sa-region shift produced exactly twice as many pages as Tuesday's shift.
12. The Auth shift was on Monday.
13. The ap-region shift produced more pages than the af-region shift.
14. Monday's shift produced more pages than Thursday's shift.

Deliverables:

A. The full 5x5 solution table with columns Day, Engineer, Service, Region, Pages, rows Monday through Friday.
B. A deduction trace. Present it as a numbered sequence of inference steps. Every step must cite the clue number(s) and the previously derived facts it uses, and must state what it concludes. No step may involve guessing followed by later verification unless you explicitly label it as a case split and then close every branch.
