C. A uniqueness proof. It is not enough to find an assignment that satisfies all fourteen clues; you must show no other assignment does. In particular, at the two points in the deduction where a case split is genuinely necessary, enumerate all branches and show explicitly which clue kills each dead branch, quoting the contradiction. If your deduction has no case splits at all, say so and justify that every step was forced.
D. Redundancy analysis. Determine which of the fourteen clues are REDUNDANT, meaning the remaining thirteen still admit exactly one solution. For each clue you claim is redundant, you must justify it (re-derive the fact it provides from the others). For each clue you claim is NOT redundant, exhibit a SECOND complete assignment that satisfies the other thirteen clues but violates that one. This part is the bulk of the work - be systematic, and go through all fourteen.
E. Finally: clue 14 was added late by the roster tool. Determine whether the puzzle has a unique solution without clue 14. If it does not, give both solutions in full.

prompts.title: SLDNF resolution and floundering
prompts.text:
Consider the following logic program, written in standard Prolog syntax. Assume a conventional SLD resolution engine with depth-first search, left-to-right goal selection, clauses tried in the order written, negation implemented as negation-as-failure (\+), and no tabling or occurs check.

  edge(a, b).
  edge(b, c).
  edge(c, d).
  edge(d, b).
  edge(a, e).
  edge(e, f).

  path(X, Y) :- edge(X, Y).
  path(X, Y) :- edge(X, Z), path(Z, Y).

  blocked(c).
  blocked(f).

  clear(X, Y) :- path(X, Y), \+ blocked(Y).

  unsafe(X) :- edge(X, c).
  safe(X) :- \+ unsafe(X).

  firstedge(X, Y) :- edge(X, Y), !.

  reach(X, X).
  reach(X, Y) :- reach(X, Z), edge(Z, Y).

Answer every one of the following. For each query, state the exact outcome: the sequence of answer substitutions in the order the engine produces them, or 'fails', or 'does not terminate'. When you say 'does not terminate', you must exhibit the repeating goal pattern that proves it - name the goals in the infinite branch.

1. ?- path(a, d).
2. ?- path(b, b).
3. ?- path(f, a).
4. ?- path(a, g).
5. ?- clear(a, d).
6. ?- clear(a, f).
7. ?- clear(a, Y).   (list every answer in engine order, and say whether it terminates after the last one)
8. ?- safe(b).
9. ?- safe(e).
10. ?- safe(X).      (this one is the trap - answer very carefully)
11. ?- firstedge(a, Y).
12. ?- firstedge(a, e).
13. ?- \+ firstedge(a, e).
14. ?- reach(a, f).
15. ?- reach(a, g).

Then the analysis:

A. Query 10 is an instance of FLOUNDERING. Explain precisely what floundering is, why the engine's answer to query 10 is not the answer that the intended reading of 'safe' would give, and state what the correct set of safe atoms is under the closed-world assumption over the Herbrand base restricted to the constants {a, b, c, d, e, f}. Give that set explicitly.
B. Compare queries 12 and 13 and explain, in terms of the cut's effect on the choice-point stack, why the pair behaves the way it does. State whether firstedge is a sound implementation of 'Y is the first edge out of X' and give the query that demonstrates the unsoundness if there is one.
C. Predicate reach is left-recursive while path is right-recursive, and both are intended to compute reachability. Compare them on queries 14 and 15 and explain the difference in operational behaviour. Then state whether they have the same LEAST HERBRAND MODEL, and prove your answer - this distinguishes declarative from operational semantics and is the point of the exercise.
D. Compute the least Herbrand model of the definite (negation-free) part of the program: list every ground atom of edge/2, path/2, reach/2 and blocked/1 that is in it. There are finitely many; enumerate the path/2 atoms in full, which requires you to work out the reachability relation of the graph exactly.
E. Give a minimal edit to the program (adding or reordering at most three lines) that makes query 4 terminate with 'fails' and query 15 terminate with 'fails', without changing any of the answers to queries 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 14. State the edit and justify that the listed answers are unchanged.

prompts.title: Seven claims about spanning trees
prompts.text:
Below are seven assertions about minimum spanning trees. All graphs are finite, simple, connected, undirected, and have positive real edge weights. Some assertions are theorems and some are false. For each: give the verdict, then a complete proof or an explicit minimal counterexample with all weights and a full verification (list the spanning trees and their totals where relevant).

C1. If all edge weights are distinct, then for every vertex v the lightest edge incident to v belongs to the minimum spanning tree.

C2. If all edge weights are distinct, then for every vertex v of degree at least 2, the SECOND-lightest edge incident to v belongs to the minimum spanning tree.

C3. If a graph has a unique minimum spanning tree, then all of its edge weights are distinct.

C4. If all edge weights are distinct, then for every cycle C in the graph, the heaviest edge of C is in no minimum spanning tree.

C5. If all edge weights are distinct, the minimum spanning tree is unique.

C6. Define a minimum bottleneck spanning tree (MBST) as a spanning tree minimizing the weight of its heaviest edge. Every MBST is a minimum spanning tree.

C7. Every minimum spanning tree is a minimum bottleneck spanning tree.

Additional requirements:

1. For C2, your counterexample must be MINIMAL in the number of vertices. Prove minimality: show that no graph on fewer vertices can refute C2 (handle each smaller vertex count explicitly).
2. For C4 and C5, the proofs should share machinery. State and prove the CUT PROPERTY and the CYCLE PROPERTY as lemmas first, with the exchange argument written out (take an MST not containing the light cut edge, add it, find the cycle it creates, identify the edge to remove, compare weights, conclude). Then derive C1, C4 and C5 from the lemmas.
3. For C3, your counterexample must exhibit a graph with at least one repeated weight and a provably unique MST. Prove the uniqueness by enumerating all spanning trees of your graph and their totals.
4. For C6, give a 4-vertex counterexample, enumerate ALL of its spanning trees with their bottleneck values and their total weights, and point out the tree that is an MBST but not an MST.
5. For C7, give the full proof. The natural route is by contradiction: assume an MST T is not an MBST, so some spanning tree T' has a strictly smaller bottleneck; consider the heaviest edge e of T and show it can be exchanged. Be careful about ties and about the case where several edges of T attain the maximum.
6. Now a synthesis question. Suppose weights are NOT distinct. State the correct generalization of C5, i.e. the precise necessary and sufficient condition on the weight function for the MST to be unique, and prove it. (Hint: it is a condition about every cut and every cycle, not merely about distinctness; state it as two conditions and prove both directions.)
7. Finally, evaluate this operational claim and prove or refute it: 'Running Kruskal and Prim on the same graph with the same tie-breaking rule on equal weights always produces the same tree.' Define what 'the same tie-breaking rule' means precisely before you answer, because the claim's truth depends on it.

prompts.title: Invariants and unreachability
prompts.text:
Four reachability questions. Each one is settled by finding the right invariant. For each, state the invariant explicitly as a function of the state, prove it is preserved by every legal move, and then use it. Where a state IS reachable, you must give an explicit construction, not just an argument that no invariant forbids it.

PART A - the blackboard.
The integers 1, 2, 3, ..., 2025 are written on a blackboard. A move consists of erasing any two numbers a and b and writing the single number |a - b| in their place. After 2024 moves exactly one number remains.
  A1. Prove that the parity of the final number is the same for every possible sequence of moves, and determine that parity. Compute the relevant sum exactly and show the arithmetic.
  A2. Prove an upper bound on the final number and state it.
  A3. Show that the final number can equal 1, by giving an explicit strategy (describe it as a general procedure and verify the counting).
  A4. Determine whether the final number can equal 2025. If yes, give the explicit strategy; if no, prove it impossible.
  A5. Determine the complete set of achievable final values and prove your characterization in both directions.

PART B - the frog on the lattice.
A frog stands at the point (2, 4) in the integer plane. From (x, y) it may jump to any of (x + y, y), (x, x + y), (x - y, y), or (x, y - x).
  B1. Exhibit an invariant of the motion and prove it is preserved by all four moves. Be careful with the case where a coordinate becomes 0 or negative; state your convention for gcd with 0 and with negative numbers.
  B2. Decide whether (6, 2026) is reachable. If yes, give an explicit jump sequence (you may describe it via the Euclidean algorithm run backwards, but then also give the first six concrete jumps).
  B3. Decide whether (3, 9) is reachable, with proof.
  B4. Decide whether (0, 0) is reachable, with proof. Then decide whether (2, 0) is reachable, with proof. Note that these two have different answers and the reason is the exact point of the exercise.
  B5. Characterize the full reachable set from (2, 4) and prove both inclusions. State the characterization as a set-builder expression.

PART C - refuting a plausible bound.
A student writes: 'In Part A, every move replaces two numbers by their absolute difference, and |a - b| is at most max(a, b) - min(a, b) <= 2025 - 1 = 2024. Therefore the final number is at most 2024.' Identify the exact logical error in this argument (it is not an arithmetic slip), and refute the conclusion using your answer to A4.

PART D - the three piles.
Three piles contain 5, 7 and 9 tokens. A legal move removes one token from each of two different piles and adds two tokens to the remaining pile.
  D1. Give an invariant and prove it preserved.
  D2. Decide whether the position (0, 0, 21) is reachable, in any assignment of those numbers to the three piles. Prove your answer, covering all orderings.
  D3. Decide whether (1, 1, 19) is reachable, and whether (2, 8, 11) is reachable. Give explicit move sequences for any that are reachable.
  D4. Characterize exactly which triples (a, b, c) with a + b + c = 21 and a, b, c >= 0 are reachable from (5, 7, 9), and prove the characterization. State how many such triples there are in total and how many are reachable; both numbers should be exact integers.

prompts.title: CTL model checking by hand
prompts.text:
Model-check the following Kripke structure by hand. Do not simulate; use the standard labeling algorithm and show the fixpoint iterations.

States: s0, s1, s2, s3, s4, s5.
Initial state: s0.
Transition relation (total - every state has at least one successor):
  s0 -> s1
  s0 -> s2
  s1 -> s3
  s2 -> s2
  s2 -> s4
  s3 -> s0
  s3 -> s5
  s4 -> s5
  s5 -> s5
Labeling (atomic propositions p, q, r):
  L(s0) = {p}
  L(s1) = {p, q}
  L(s2) = {q}
  L(s3) = {r}
  L(s4) = {p, r}
  L(s5) = {q, r}

Task 1. For each of the following CTL formulas, compute the FULL SET of states satisfying it (not just whether s0 satisfies it). Present each as Sat(phi) = { ... }. For the formulas involving fixpoints (EU, EG, AF, AG), show the iteration sequence explicitly: the sequence of approximant sets X_0, X_1, X_2, ... until stabilization, and state how many iterations were needed.
  f1  = EF r
  f2  = AF r
  f3  = AG (EF p)
  f4  = EG q
  f5  = AG (p -> AF r)
  f6  = E[p U r]
  f7  = A[p U r]
  f8  = AF (AG r)
  f9  = AG (AF r)
  f10 = EG (AF q)
  f11 = AF (p AND q)
  f12 = E[q U (p AND r)]

Task 2. State clearly, for each of f1 through f12, whether the INITIAL state s0 satisfies it. Present this as a table.

Task 3. The formulas f8 = AF AG r and f9 = AG AF r are not equivalent in general. Using your computed sets, state whether this structure separates them (i.e. whether some state satisfies one and not the other). If it does, name the state and explain what path witnesses the difference. If it does not, MODIFY the structure by adding or removing exactly one transition so that it does, present the modified structure, and recompute Sat(f8) and Sat(f9) for it.

Task 4. Express f2, f5 and f9 using only the adequate set of CTL operators {EX, EU, EG} together with boolean connectives, and verify one of your rewrites by recomputing its satisfaction set from the rewritten form and checking it matches the answer from Task 1.

Task 5. Fairness. Impose the fairness constraint 'infinitely often q'. Under fair CTL semantics (only fair paths are considered), recompute Sat(f2) and Sat(f9). Identify which states have at least one fair path at all, since states with no fair path satisfy no existential formula and vacuously satisfy universal ones - be explicit about that.

Task 6. Two claims to adjudicate. For each, prove or refute using this structure:
  (a) 'In any Kripke structure, AG AF r implies AF AG r.'

  pub struct SystemClock;             // impl Clock using Instant::now()
  pub struct MockClock { ... }        // interior mutability, pub fn advance(&self, d: Duration)

  pub enum Decision { Allow { remaining: u32 }, Deny { retry_after_millis: u64 } }
  pub trait RateLimiter {

prompts.title: Python dependency resolver package
prompts.text:
Write a small but real Python package that resolves package version constraints, then prove it works. Output every file completely, each introduced by its path. Target Python 3.11, standard library only (no packaging, no pip internals). Type hints throughout; the code must pass `mypy --strict` in spirit even if you cannot run it.

Files:

  pyproject.toml
  src/minresolve/__init__.py
  src/minresolve/version.py
  src/minresolve/constraints.py
  src/minresolve/resolver.py
  src/minresolve/cli.py
  tests/test_version.py
  tests/test_constraints.py
  tests/test_resolver.py
  tests/test_cli.py

Contracts between modules - honour these exactly:

version.py: `class Version` with a total ordering, parsed from strings of the form MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH with an optional pre-release suffix like `-rc.1` or `-alpha.2`. Ordering rules: numeric components compare numerically; a version with a pre-release sorts BEFORE the same version without one; pre-release identifiers compare left to right, numeric identifiers numerically and below alphanumeric ones. Implement __lt__, __eq__, __hash__, __repr__. Raise `InvalidVersion` on malformed input.

constraints.py: `class Constraint` parsed from strings like `>=1.2.0`, `<2.0.0`, `==1.4.3`, `!=1.5.0`, `~=1.4.2` (compatible release: >=1.4.2, <1.5.0), and `^1.4.2` (caret: >=1.4.2, <2.0.0, but for 0.x it is >=0.4.2, <0.5.0 - implement that special case). `class ConstraintSet` holds several constraints, supports `.allows(Version) -> bool`, `.intersect(other) -> ConstraintSet`, and `.is_empty() -> bool`. Pre-releases are excluded unless the constraint set explicitly mentions a pre-release version - implement and document that rule.

resolver.py: `def resolve(root_requirements: dict[str, str], index: dict[str, dict[str, dict[str, str]]]) -> dict[str, Version]`. `index` maps package name -> version string -> that version's own requirements (name -> constraint string). Use backtracking with these rules: always try the highest allowed version first; on conflict, backjump to the package that caused the conflict rather than the most recent decision; raise `ResolutionImpossible` carrying the conflicting requirement chain when no solution exists. Include a deterministic tie-break so the same input always yields the same output.

cli.py: `python -m minresolve resolve --manifest FILE [--json] [--verbose]` reading a JSON manifest with keys `requirements` and `index`. Exit code 0 on success, 2 on `ResolutionImpossible` (printing the conflict chain to stderr), 3 on a malformed manifest. Uses argparse; the entry point is `main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int` so tests can call it directly.

Tests must include, at minimum: version ordering including `1.0.0-rc.1 < 1.0.0` and `1.0.0-alpha.2 < 1.0.0-alpha.10`; caret behaviour for `^0.4.2`; an intersect that is empty; a resolution requiring backtracking at least two levels deep (construct the index so a naive greedy 'take highest' fails and must undo two decisions); a diamond dependency with a satisfiable overlap; an unsatisfiable case asserting on the exact conflict chain; and a CLI test using capsys and a tmp_path manifest asserting exit codes 0, 2 and 3.

After the code, answer: what is the worst-case complexity of your resolver, what concrete input shape triggers it, and which single change would give the biggest practical speedup? Keep that answer under 200 words.

- (endpoint_id, idempotency_key) is globally unique.
- attempt_count >= 0 and attempt_count <= 12, enforced by a CHECK constraint.
- next_attempt_at must be NULL exactly when status is in (succeeded, failed_permanent), enforced by a CHECK constraint. Write that constraint correctly - the naive version is wrong for NULL comparisons; get it right and explain.

Set down_revision = '0006_add_endpoint_secret'.

  class WebhookDeliveryRepository:
      def __init__(self, session: Session) -> None
      def enqueue(self, endpoint_id: UUID, idempotency_key: str, payload: dict) -> tuple[WebhookDelivery, bool]
      def claim_batch(self, now: datetime, limit: int) -> list[WebhookDelivery]

      def mark_failed(self, delivery_id: UUID, error: str, backoff: timedelta) -> None

Behavioural contract:
- enqueue returns (row, created) and is idempotent on (endpoint_id, idempotency_key). Implement it with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING plus a re-select, NOT with a try/except IntegrityError around a plain insert, and explain in a comment why the SELECT-then-INSERT pattern is racy under READ COMMITTED.

prompts.title: Go circuit breaker package
prompts.text:
I need a production-quality circuit breaker in Go, delivered as a set of files. Print each file in full, prefixed by its path. Go 1.22, no third-party dependencies except the standard library and `github.com/google/go-cmp` in tests.

Files:

  breaker/clock.go
  breaker/counting.go
  breaker/rolling.go
  breaker/breaker_test.go
  breaker/rolling_test.go

breaker/clock.go: a `Clock` interface with `Now() time.Time` and `AfterFunc(d time.Duration, f func()) Timer`, a `realClock`, and a `FakeClock` supporting `Advance(d time.Duration)` that fires due timers deterministically in timestamp order. Getting FakeClock right is half the exercise: timers scheduled by a timer callback during Advance must be handled correctly. State your rule (do they fire within the same Advance or not?) and be consistent.

breaker/breaker.go: 
  type State int  // StateClosed, StateOpen, StateHalfOpen, with a String() method
  type Policy interface {
      RecordSuccess(now time.Time)
      RecordFailure(now time.Time)
      ShouldTrip(now time.Time) bool
      Reset()
      Snapshot() Counts
  }
  type Counts struct{ Successes, Failures, Total uint64; FailureRatio float64 }
  type Breaker struct { ... }
  func New(p Policy, opts ...Option) *Breaker
  func (b *Breaker) Do(ctx context.Context, fn func(context.Context) error) error
  var ErrOpen = errors.New("circuit breaker is open")
Options: WithClock(Clock), WithOpenTimeout(time.Duration), WithHalfOpenMaxInFlight(int), WithIsFailure(func(error) bool), WithOnStateChange(func(from, to State)).
Semantics you must implement exactly: in StateOpen, Do returns ErrOpen without calling fn; after OpenTimeout elapses the breaker moves to StateHalfOpen; in StateHalfOpen at most HalfOpenMaxInFlight calls run concurrently and further calls get ErrOpen; a single failure in half-open reopens and restarts the timeout; HalfOpenMaxInFlight consecutive successes close it. Context cancellation must NOT be counted as a failure by default - implement that in the default IsFailure and explain why it matters.

breaker/counting.go: `CountingPolicy` - trips when failures >= N within the last M total calls (a simple consecutive-or-quota rule you define precisely in a doc comment).
breaker/rolling.go: `RollingPolicy` - a bucketed sliding window: W buckets each covering D duration, trips when the failure ratio over the window exceeds R AND total calls over the window >= MinimumRequests. Implement bucket rotation without allocating per call, and handle a gap where no calls happened for longer than the whole window (all buckets must be considered stale and zeroed - the naive rotation loop is O(W) worst case; that is fine, but the naive version that only rotates one bucket is a bug, so do not write it).

Tests: table-driven, using FakeClock only, no sleeps anywhere. Cover: closed to open transition at the exact threshold and one below it; open returning ErrOpen without invoking fn (assert an invocation counter stayed at zero); the transition to half-open at exactly OpenTimeout and at OpenTimeout minus 1ns; half-open concurrency cap enforced with goroutines and a WaitGroup; a half-open failure reopening; bucket rotation across a window boundary and across a full-window gap; and OnStateChange callbacks firing in the right order with the right (from, to) pairs.

After the code answer three questions briefly: (1) which mutex covers what, and whether Snapshot can return a torn view; (2) what happens if fn panics and how you handle it; (3) why `sync.RWMutex` would or would not help here, with reasoning about the actual critical-section cost.

Deliver a vertical slice of a TypeScript HTTP API. Output every file completely with its path as a heading. Node 20, ESM, TypeScript 5.4 with `strict: true` and `noUncheckedIndexedAccess: true`, Express 4, Zod 3, Vitest, and no other runtime dependencies.

The domain: seat reservations for events. A reservation has id, eventId, userId, seatIds (a non-empty array of strings, max 8, no duplicates), holdExpiresAt (ISO timestamp), and state ('held' | 'confirmed' | 'released').

Contracts:

domain/errors.ts exports a discriminated error hierarchy: `AppError` base with a `code` literal union, and subclasses SeatUnavailableError (carrying the conflicting seatIds), ReservationNotFoundError, ReservationExpiredError, InvalidStateTransitionError (carrying from and to). services/reservation.service.ts holds the business rules: creating a reservation calls tryHoldSeats and throws SeatUnavailableError with the conflicts on failure; confirming requires state 'held' and holdExpiresAt strictly in the future, otherwise ReservationExpiredError; confirming an already-confirmed reservation is idempotent and returns the existing one; confirming a released one throws InvalidStateTransitionError. prompts.title: C ring buffer with fuzz harness
prompts.text:
Write a single-producer single-consumer lock-free ring buffer in C11, plus its tests and a fuzz harness. Output each file complete, with its path as a heading. No dependencies beyond the C standard library, <stdatomic.h>, and pthreads for the threaded test.

Files:
  include/spsc_ring.h
  src/spsc_ring.c
  test/test_spsc_ring.c
  fuzz/fuzz_spsc_ring.c
  Makefile

API in include/spsc_ring.h:
  typedef struct spsc_ring spsc_ring;
  spsc_ring *spsc_ring_create(size_t capacity_bytes);   /* rounded UP to a power of two; returns NULL on failure */
  void spsc_ring_destroy(spsc_ring *r);
  size_t spsc_ring_write(spsc_ring *r, const void *buf, size_t n);  /* returns bytes written, 0..n, never blocks */
  size_t spsc_ring_read(spsc_ring *r, void *buf, size_t n);         /* returns bytes read, 0..n, never blocks */
  size_t spsc_ring_readable(const spsc_ring *r);
  size_t spsc_ring_writable(const spsc_ring *r);
  /* framed layer, built on the byte layer */
  int spsc_ring_write_frame(spsc_ring *r, const void *buf, uint32_t n); /* all-or-nothing; 0 on success, -1 if insufficient space */
  int spsc_ring_read_frame(spsc_ring *r, void *buf, uint32_t cap, uint32_t *out_n); /* 0 ok, -1 no complete frame, -2 buffer too small */

Implementation requirements you must actually satisfy, not just claim:
1. Power-of-two capacity with masked indices, and monotonically increasing head/tail counters so that full and empty are distinguishable without wasting a slot. State the exact expressions for readable and writable and prove they are correct across the counter wraparound of size_t.
2. Correct memory ordering: the producer publishes with release, the consumer acquires. Say exactly which loads and stores are relaxed and which are not, and explain what breaks if the release on the write index is downgraded to relaxed. Do not use seq_cst everywhere.
3. False sharing avoided: head and tail on separate cache lines using alignas(64), with a comment on why.
4. The framed layer writes a 4-byte little-endian length prefix. It must be all-or-nothing even though the byte layer is partial-write: implement it by checking writable() first, and explain why that check is sound for SPSC but would be unsound for MPSC.
5. Handle the wraparound copy correctly: a write that straddles the end of the storage becomes two memcpys. Get the split sizes right; this is the classic off-by-one.

test/test_spsc_ring.c: a hand-rolled assertion harness (no framework). Cover: capacity rounding (ask for 100, expect 128); fill exactly to capacity then assert writable() == 0 and a further write returns 0; read exactly to empty; a straddling write/read pair verified byte by byte with a known pattern; framed round-trip including a frame that straddles; read_frame returning -1 when only the length prefix has been written; read_frame returning -2 with the frame left intact (assert a subsequent call with a big enough buffer still succeeds - this is the subtle requirement); and a two-thread test pushing 10 million bytes of a pseudo-random pattern through a 4096-byte ring, verifying the consumer's checksum matches.

fuzz/fuzz_spsc_ring.c: an LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput that interprets the input as an opcode stream (create with size, write n bytes, read n bytes, write_frame, read_frame) and maintains a shadow model - a simple std-C queue - asserting after every operation that readable() matches the model's length and that read data matches the model byte for byte. Include the exact invariants you assert.

Makefile: targets `test` (with -fsanitize=address,undefined -Wall -Wextra -Werror), `tsan` (-fsanitize=thread for the threaded test), and `fuzz` (clang -fsanitize=fuzzer,address).

Afterwards, answer: is your implementation correct if the two threads run on different NUMA nodes, and would ThreadSanitizer flag anything in a correct implementation of this pattern? Justify.

api.py defines the extension points as Protocols (typing.Protocol, runtime_checkable where it makes sense):
  class Parser(Protocol):
      name: str
      def sniff(self, sample: bytes) -> float: ...      # confidence 0.0-1.0
      def parse(self, line: bytes) -> dict[str, object] | None: ...
  class Filter(Protocol):
      name: str
      def keep(self, record: dict[str, object]) -> bool: ...

Tests must include a conftest fixture that fabricates entry points WITHOUT installing packages (monkeypatch importlib.metadata.entry_points), covering: lazy loading verified by an import-side-effect flag; the priority conflict; the equal-priority DuplicatePluginError; a plugin that raises on import; sniff-based auto-selection where the JSONL parser wins over syslog on JSON input and loses on syslog input; the filter-raises path with exact counters; and the sink-raises abort path asserting close() was still called.

6. tests/singular/assert_revenue_matches_source.sql must reconcile total revenue in the mart against the raw table for the trailing 30 days, tolerating only rows explicitly excluded by a documented rule (e.g. status = 'cancelled'), and must fail loudly otherwise. Write the tolerance as an explicit predicate, not a fuzzy percentage.

After the code, answer three questions: (a) exactly what your incremental model does on a full-refresh versus an incremental run and whether history is reproducible; (b) what happens if the same customer_event is delivered twice with identical event_ts and different email, and which of your constraints catches it; (c) the query cost implication of your surrogate key choice (hash versus concatenated natural key) on a table of 900 million rows.

prompts.title: Debug and repair four files
prompts.text:
The four files below are a working-ish job scheduler that has three separate bugs, at least one of which is a genuine concurrency bug that a single-threaded test will never catch. Find them all, then output CORRECTED versions of every file in full plus a new regression test file. Do not output diffs; output complete files. Python 3.11.

===== scheduler/queue.py =====
import heapq, threading, time
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Any

@dataclass(order=True)
class Job:
    run_at: float
    priority: int
    seq: int = field(compare=True)
    payload: Any = field(compare=False, default=None)

class DelayQueue:
    def __init__(self):
        self._heap: list[Job] = []
        self._lock = threading.Lock()
        self._cv = threading.Condition(self._lock)
        self._seq = 0
        self._closed = False

    def put(self, payload, delay: float, priority: int = 0) -> None:
        with self._lock:
            if self._closed:
                raise RuntimeError("queue closed")
            self._seq += 1
            job = Job(run_at=time.monotonic() + delay, priority=priority, seq=self._seq, payload=payload)
            heapq.heappush(self._heap, job)
            self._cv.notify()

    def get(self, timeout: float | None = None):
        deadline = None if timeout is None else time.monotonic() + timeout
        with self._cv:
            while True:
                if self._closed and not self._heap:
                    return None
                if self._heap:
                    job = self._heap[0]
                    now = time.monotonic()
                    if job.run_at <= now:
                        heapq.heappop(self._heap)
                        return job
                    wait = job.run_at - now
                else:
                    wait = timeout
                if deadline is not None and time.monotonic() >= deadline:
                    return None
                self._cv.wait(wait)

    def close(self) -> None:
        with self._lock:
            self._closed = True
            self._cv.notify()

===== scheduler/worker.py =====
import threading, logging
from .queue import DelayQueue

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

class WorkerPool:
    def __init__(self, q: DelayQueue, handler, size: int = 4, max_retries: int = 3):
        self.q = q
        self.handler = handler
        self.size = size
        self.max_retries = max_retries
        self._threads = []
        self._stop = threading.Event()
        self.processed = 0
        self.failed = 0

    def start(self):
        for i in range(self.size):
            t = threading.Thread(target=self._run, name=f"worker-{i}", daemon=True)
            t.start()
            self._threads.append(t)

    def _run(self):
        while not self._stop.is_set():
            job = self.q.get(timeout=0.5)
            if job is None:
                continue
            attempt = getattr(job, "attempt", 0)
            try:
                self.handler(job.payload)
                self.processed += 1
            except Exception:
                log.exception("job failed")
                if attempt < self.max_retries:
                    job.attempt = attempt + 1
                    self.q.put(job.payload, delay=2 ** attempt, priority=job.priority)
                else:
                    self.failed += 1

    def stop(self, timeout: float = 5.0):
        self._stop.set()
        self.q.close()
        for t in self._threads:
            t.join(timeout)

===== scheduler/dedupe.py =====
import time, threading

class Deduplicator:
    def __init__(self, ttl: float = 60.0, max_size: int = 10000):
        self.ttl = ttl
        self.max_size = max_size
        self._seen: dict[str, float] = {}
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def check_and_add(self, key: str) -> bool:
        now = time.monotonic()
        with self._lock:
            if len(self._seen) > self.max_size:
                for k, ts in list(self._seen.items()):
                    if now - ts > self.ttl:
                        del self._seen[k]
            prev = self._seen.get(key)
            if prev is not None and now - prev < self.ttl:
                return False
            self._seen[key] = now
            return True

===== scheduler/__init__.py =====
from .queue import DelayQueue, Job
from .worker import WorkerPool
from .dedupe import Deduplicator

__all__ = ["DelayQueue", "Job", "WorkerPool", "Deduplicator"]

===== end of files =====

What to produce:

1. A bug report listing each defect with: the file and the specific line or construct, what goes wrong, the precise conditions under which it manifests, and the observable symptom in production. There are at least three real defects. Rank them by severity and justify the ranking. Be careful to distinguish real bugs from stylistic issues - do not pad the list.
2. Corrected versions of scheduler/queue.py, scheduler/worker.py, scheduler/dedupe.py and scheduler/__init__.py, complete.
3. A new file tests/test_scheduler.py with pytest tests that FAIL against the original code and PASS against your corrected code. For the concurrency bug you must write a test that reliably reproduces it - explain your technique for making it deterministic (barriers, monkeypatched time, forced thread interleaving) rather than relying on chance. A flaky test does not count.
4. State whether the priority field is actually honoured by DelayQueue as written, and if not, what the correct ordering key should be to honour 'earliest run_at, then highest priority, then FIFO'. Note that Python's heapq is a min-heap; get the sign right.
5. Say which of the bugs would be caught by mypy --strict, which by a thread sanitizer equivalent, and which only by a targeted test.

prompts.title: SDTP specification conformance review
prompts.text:
Below is the full text of an internal draft specification. Read all of it, then perform the review task described after the document. Cite section numbers for every claim you make.

================ BEGIN DOCUMENT ================

DRAFT-SDTP-11: Segmented Delta Transfer Protocol, Version 1.1
Status: Working Draft, superseding DRAFT-SDTP-09 (version 1.0)
Editors: R. Okonkwo, M. Falk, S. Reyes

1. Introduction

The Segmented Delta Transfer Protocol (SDTP) is a bidirectional, connection-oriented protocol for transferring large mutable objects between a Producer and a Consumer over a reliable byte stream (typically TCP or a QUIC stream). SDTP is designed for the case where the Consumer already holds a prior revision of the object and only the differences need to be transferred. SDTP version 1.0 was deployed in production between March and November of last year; version 1.1 adds compression negotiation, credit-based flow control, and a revised error taxonomy.

This document uses the key words MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, and MAY as defined in the usual normative-language conventions.

2. Terminology

Object: an addressable blob identified by a 16-octet ObjectID.
Revision: a monotonically increasing 64-bit integer associated with an Object. Revisions are assigned by the Producer.
Segment: a contiguous byte range of an Object at a given Revision. Segments are the unit of delta computation.
Base: the Revision that the Consumer holds and against which a delta is computed.
Session: a sequence of frames exchanged over one transport connection.
Credit: the number of octets the sender is permitted to transmit without further authorization.

3. Message Framing

All SDTP messages are carried in frames. Every frame begins with a fixed 12-octet header:

  offset 0, 1 octet:   Frame Type
  offset 1, 3 octets:  Payload Length, unsigned, network byte order
  offset 4, 4 octets:  Sequence Number, unsigned, network byte order
  offset 8, 4 octets:  Stream Identifier, unsigned, network byte order

The Payload Length field is 24 bits wide and therefore encodes payload sizes from 0 to 16,777,215 octets inclusive. A receiver MUST reject a frame whose declared Payload Length exceeds the value advertised in the peer's HELLO frame, with error 0x03.

Sequence Numbers are per Stream Identifier, begin at 1 for the first frame sent on a stream, and increase by exactly 1 for each subsequent frame. Sequence Numbers wrap to 0 after 4,294,967,295. Receivers MUST detect gaps in the Sequence Number space and MUST NOT process a frame whose Sequence Number is less than the highest previously processed Sequence Number on that stream.

Frame Types defined in this version: 0x01 HELLO, 0x02 VERSION, 0x03 REQUEST, 0x04 MANIFEST, 0x05 SEGMENT, 0x06 CREDIT, 0x07 ACK, 0x08 NACK, 0x09 CLOSE, 0x0A PING, 0x0B PONG.

4. Session Establishment

Upon connection, each endpoint MUST send a HELLO frame as the first frame on stream 0. The HELLO frame carries the sender's maximum acceptable Payload Length, the initial Credit window, the list of supported compression algorithms, and a 32-octet random nonce. A session is established when both endpoints have sent and received a HELLO.

The initial Credit window advertised in HELLO SHOULD be 64 KiB. An endpoint MUST NOT send more than the peer's advertised initial Credit before receiving the first CREDIT frame.

An endpoint that receives any frame other than HELLO as the first frame of a session MUST close the connection with error 0x01.

5. Delta Negotiation

The Consumer initiates a transfer by sending a REQUEST frame containing an ObjectID, the Revision it desires (or 0 for 'latest'), and the Base Revision it currently holds. The Producer replies with a MANIFEST frame enumerating the Segments that differ between the Base and the target Revision. Each manifest entry contains a segment index, an offset, a length, and a 32-bit checksum of the segment content at the target Revision.

If the Producer no longer retains the Base Revision, it SHOULD reply with a MANIFEST that enumerates every Segment of the object, effectively degrading to a full transfer. The Producer MAY instead reply with error 0x05 (BASE_UNAVAILABLE).

A Consumer MAY request a delta against a Base Revision for which it holds only a partial copy. In such cases the Producer computes the delta against the complete Base Revision as it exists on the Producer.

Segment indices in a MANIFEST are ordered by ascending offset. A Producer MUST NOT emit two manifest entries with overlapping byte ranges.

6. Flow Control

SDTP uses credit-based flow control at the session level. The initial credit is 65,535 octets. A receiver replenishes credit by sending a CREDIT frame containing the number of additional octets it is willing to accept. Credit is cumulative and saturates at 2^31 - 1.

Implementations MUST support the transmission and reception of frames with payloads up to 32 MiB in order to accommodate large segment transfers efficiently. Senders SHOULD prefer payload sizes between 16 KiB and 256 KiB.

A sender that exhausts its credit MUST stop transmitting SEGMENT frames but MAY continue to send PING, CREDIT, and CLOSE frames.

7. Retransmission and Recovery

Although SDTP runs over a reliable transport, application-level recovery is required for the case where the Producer restarts mid-transfer or a proxy truncates a stream.

If a Consumer has not received a SEGMENT frame it expects within 3 round-trip times of the last received frame on the stream, it MUST send a NACK frame naming the missing segment indices. The Producer MUST retransmit the named segments within one round-trip time or reply with error 0x08.

A Consumer MUST send an ACK frame after every 16 SEGMENT frames received, or after 500 milliseconds have elapsed since the last ACK, whichever comes first. ACK frames carry the highest contiguous Sequence Number received.

When comparing Sequence Numbers for the purpose of gap detection, implementations perform unsigned comparison.

8. Compression

HELLO advertises supported compression algorithms in preference order. The algorithms defined are: 0x00 none, 0x01 deflate, 0x02 zstd, 0x03 brotli. The Producer selects the first algorithm in its own preference list that also appears in the Consumer's list, and names it in the MANIFEST frame.

Compression is applied to SEGMENT payloads only. Frame headers are never compressed. When a session is protected by TLS, compression MUST be applied after encryption to avoid compression-oracle attacks.

A SEGMENT frame carrying compressed data sets bit 7 of the Frame Type octet. The Payload Length field reflects the compressed length.

9. Security Considerations

SDTP does not define its own cryptography and relies on the underlying transport. Deployments SHOULD use TLS 1.3 or a QUIC stream. The 32-octet nonce in HELLO is intended for use in channel binding by a future version and is currently unused; implementations MUST include it and MUST NOT rely on it.

Because compression is applied to attacker-influenceable content, deployments handling secrets alongside attacker-controlled data SHOULD disable compression. See section 8 for the ordering requirement relative to encryption.

10. IANA Considerations

This document requests registration of TCP port 7414 and the establishment of an SDTP Frame Type registry with the initial contents listed in section 3. Values 0x80 through 0xFF are reserved for private use.

11. Error Codes

  0x01 UNEXPECTED_FRAME - a frame arrived that is not permitted in the current session state.
  0x02 VERSION_UNSUPPORTED - no mutually supported protocol version.
  0x03 FRAME_TOO_LARGE - declared Payload Length exceeds the peer's advertised maximum.
  0x04 UNKNOWN_OBJECT - the requested ObjectID is not known to the Producer.
  0x05 BASE_UNAVAILABLE - the requested Base Revision is no longer retained.
  0x06 CHECKSUM_MISMATCH - a received segment failed checksum validation.
  0x07 CREDIT_VIOLATION - the peer transmitted beyond its available credit.
  0x08 RETRANSMIT_FAILED - the Producer cannot satisfy a NACK. Producers SHOULD send this if a retransmission cannot be completed within 2 round-trip times of receiving the NACK.
  0x09 COMPRESSION_ERROR - decompression failed.
  0x0A INTERNAL - unspecified failure.

An endpoint sending an error MUST follow it with a CLOSE frame and MUST NOT send further frames.

12. Version Negotiation and Backward Compatibility

An endpoint that supports multiple protocol versions MAY send a VERSION frame prior to HELLO listing the versions it supports. If the peer does not respond with a VERSION frame within one round-trip time, the endpoint MUST assume version 1.0 and proceed.

Version 1.0 endpoints do not implement CREDIT frames. A 1.1 endpoint communicating with a 1.0 endpoint MUST disable flow control and MUST NOT send CREDIT frames. Because 1.0 endpoints reject unknown frame types with error 0x01, sending a CREDIT frame to a 1.0 peer terminates the session.

13. Appendix A: Example Trace

The following trace was captured from a 1.1 Consumer talking to a 1.1 Producer. Frames are listed as (direction, type, stream, seqno, notes).

  C->P  VERSION  stream 0  seq 1   lists [1.1, 1.0]
  P->C  HELLO    stream 0  seq 1   maxpayload 1048576, credit 65536, algos [zstd, deflate, none]
  C->P  HELLO    stream 0  seq 2   maxpayload 262144, credit 65535, algos [deflate, none]
  P->C  VERSION  stream 0  seq 2   lists [1.1]
  C->P  REQUEST  stream 4  seq 1   object 0x9f..., revision 0, base 4471
  P->C  MANIFEST stream 4  seq 2   17 segments, algorithm deflate
  P->C  SEGMENT  stream 4  seq 3   32768 octets compressed
  P->C  SEGMENT  stream 4  seq 4   65536 octets compressed
  ...   (13 more SEGMENT frames)
  C->P  ACK      stream 4  seq 2   highest contiguous 18
  P->C  SEGMENT  stream 4  seq 20  524288 octets compressed
  C->P  NACK     stream 4  seq 3   missing segment index 11
  P->C  SEGMENT  stream 4  seq 21  retransmission of index 11
  C->P  CLOSE    stream 0  seq 3

================ END DOCUMENT ================

Your task, as a specification reviewer:

1. Produce a defect list. For each defect give: a short title, the section number(s) involved, a classification from {CONTRADICTION, AMBIGUITY, UNDERSPECIFICATION, SECURITY DEFECT, EDITORIAL}, a quotation of the offending text, an explanation of the concrete interoperability failure it causes (name the two implementations and what each would do), and proposed replacement text. There are at least seven substantive defects. Find them all; do not pad with editorial nits until you have exhausted the real ones.
2. Two numeric values in the document are inconsistent with each other by exactly one octet. Identify them by section and explain which one should change and why.
3. Section 8 contains a security instruction that is backwards. State the correct ordering, explain the attack that the incorrect ordering fails to prevent AND explain why the stated ordering is also useless in the other direction (i.e. what does compressing ciphertext actually achieve).
4. Sections 7 and 11 disagree about a timeout. Give both numbers, say which section governs, and propose text that removes the ambiguity.
5. Section 3 requires gap detection with unsigned comparison, and also specifies wrapping sequence numbers. Explain precisely why these two requirements are incompatible, construct a two-frame example with concrete sequence numbers where a conformant receiver drops a valid frame, and specify the correct comparison rule.
6. Analyse the Appendix A trace against the normative text. List every frame in the trace that violates a MUST or MUST NOT, citing the section. There are at least four violations. For each, say what a strict receiver would do.
7. Section 12 describes a version negotiation scheme that cannot work. Explain the deadlock or ambiguity, and rewrite section 12 so that a 1.1 endpoint can talk to a 1.0 endpoint without either side terminating the session, without changing section 4's requirement that HELLO be first.
8. Finally, produce a state machine for the Consumer side as a table of (state, event, action, next state), covering at minimum the states DISCONNECTED, HELLO_SENT, ESTABLISHED, REQUESTED, RECEIVING, DRAINING, CLOSED. Every error code in section 11 must appear as an event somewhere in the table.

prompts.title: Reconciling three incident reports
prompts.text:
Three teams have each written up the same outage. They disagree. Read all three, then reconcile them.

================ REPORT 1 of 3: Platform SRE ================

Incident: INC-4417, 'Checkout unavailable'
Severity: SEV-1
Author: Platform SRE on-call (T. Vasquez)
Customer impact: 62 minutes of elevated checkout errors, peaking at 94% failure rate.

Timeline (all times UTC, from our alerting system):

02:11 - Automated canary deploy of checkout-api v3.44.1 begins in eu-west-1. Deploy tooling reports success at 02:14.
02:19 - First alert: checkout_5xx_rate crosses 1% in eu-west-1. Paged.
02:23 - On-call acknowledges. Dashboards show checkout-api pods in eu-west-1 with rising p99 latency (from 140 ms baseline to 2.4 s) but CPU under 30%.
02:26 - checkout_5xx_rate reaches 41%. Alert fires in us-east-1 as well, which has NOT received the new deploy. This is the first indication the problem is not deploy-local.
02:31 - We observe connection pool exhaustion errors in checkout-api logs: 'timed out acquiring connection from pool after 5000ms'. Pool size is 40 per pod, 220 pods.
02:34 - Escalated to Database team. They report the primary is healthy: CPU 38%, no long-running queries visible in pg_stat_activity beyond 400 ms.
02:38 - We initiate a rollback of v3.44.1 in eu-west-1 as a precaution. Rollback completes 02:44. No improvement; error rate now 88% globally.
02:47 - Database team reports that connection count on the primary is at 5,980 out of a max_connections of 6,000. This is the first time anyone mentions connection counts.
02:52 - We scale checkout-api DOWN from 220 to 120 pods to reduce connection pressure. Error rate drops to 51% within 90 seconds.
02:58 - Vendor (Perilune, our connection pooler) opens a status page incident acknowledging 'elevated latency in the EU region'.
03:04 - Database team restarts the Perilune pooler process on the primary. Connections drop to 210. Error rate falls below 1% within 40 seconds.
03:13 - Declared resolved after 10 minutes of clean metrics.

Our assessment: the root cause was the Perilune pooler leaking connections. The v3.44.1 deploy is a red herring - the problem appeared in us-east-1 which never received it. The 62-minute duration is attributable to 28 minutes lost pursuing the deploy hypothesis because the deploy and the first alert were 8 minutes apart.

Action items we own: (1) alert on database connection count, which we did not have; (2) stop treating temporal correlation with a deploy as causation; (3) reduce per-pod pool size from 40 to 20.

================ REPORT 2 of 3: Database Engineering ================

Postmortem: INC-4417
Author: Database Engineering (K. Nwosu)

Summary: A change in application connection behaviour introduced in checkout-api v3.44.1 caused connection exhaustion on the primary. The pooler behaved as designed.

What actually happened:

The checkout-api v3.44.1 release included a change to the order-hold code path that opens a second database session to perform an advisory lock, holds it for the duration of an external payment-gateway call, and closes it afterwards. Under normal latency this second session lives for about 180 ms. During the incident, the payment gateway was slow (see below), so these sessions lived for 8 to 30 seconds each.

We disagree with SRE's claim that us-east-1 was unaffected by the deploy. Checking our deployment records, v3.44.1 was rolled out to us-east-1 at 01:52, forty minutes BEFORE eu-west-1, as part of the standard progressive rollout. SRE's canary dashboard only tracks the eu-west-1 canary stage and does not display the earlier us-east-1 stage. The 02:26 alert in us-east-1 is therefore entirely consistent with the deploy hypothesis.

Connection accounting: at 02:47 we observed 5,980 connections. With 220 pods x 40 pooled connections = 8,800 potential, we were not near application-pool saturation; the constraint was max_connections on the primary. The advisory-lock sessions are opened OUTSIDE the application pool (they use a separate direct connection, which is the actual defect) and therefore are not bounded by the pool size at all. SRE's action item (3), reducing pool size to 20, would not have prevented this incident, and we object to it being recorded as a fix.

Regarding the payment gateway: our APM shows payment-gateway p99 latency rising from 240 ms to 11 s starting at 02:04, seven minutes before the eu-west-1 deploy and twelve minutes after the us-east-1 deploy. We believe the gateway degradation was the trigger and the v3.44.1 change was the vulnerability.

Why the restart 'fixed' it: restarting the pooler killed every session including the leaked advisory-lock sessions. This is consistent with our explanation and does not require a pooler bug.

Timeline corrections to Report 1:
- 01:52, not 02:11, is the start of the relevant deploy window.
- The 02:34 statement that 'the primary is healthy' was accurate as stated: no long queries. Long-lived IDLE IN TRANSACTION sessions are not long-running queries and would not appear as SRE seems to have expected.
- The scale-down at 02:52 helped because it reduced the number of concurrent order-hold code paths, not because it reduced pool pressure.

================ REPORT 3 of 3: Perilune (vendor) RCA ================

Root Cause Analysis provided to customer, incident PLN-2291
Prepared by Perilune Support Engineering

On the date in question our monitoring detected elevated connection-establishment latency in our EU region between 02:41 and 03:07 UTC. We have completed our investigation.

Findings:

1. Perilune pooler version 6.2.3, which the customer runs, contains a known issue (PLN-BUG-1188) in which server-side sessions in state 'idle in transaction' are not returned to the free pool and are not subject to the server_idle_timeout setting. This issue is fixed in 6.2.5, released eleven weeks before the incident. The customer's fleet is on 6.2.3.

2. During the incident window we observed 4,100 sessions in the affected state on the customer's primary. These sessions accumulated over approximately 50 minutes at a roughly linear rate.

3. Our status page entry at 02:58 referred to a separate and unrelated capacity event in our EU control plane affecting the Perilune management API. It did not affect data-path connection handling. We acknowledge that the timing was confusing and that our status page wording implied a broader impact than was the case. We have updated our status page policy.

4. We do not have visibility into what caused the customer's application to leave sessions idle in transaction. Our logs show the sessions were opened by the role 'checkout_app' and each had executed a pg_advisory_lock call before going idle.

5. The customer's max_connections is set to 6,000 while our recommended configuration for their pooler tier is 2,000 with transaction-mode pooling. The customer runs session-mode pooling, which we do not recommend at this scale and which materially amplifies the impact of PLN-BUG-1188.

Recommendations: upgrade to 6.2.5 or later; move to transaction-mode pooling; set server_idle_transaction_timeout; reduce max_connections in line with tier guidance.

Note on timing: our internal telemetry shows the first 'idle in transaction' session that was never reclaimed at 02:07 UTC.

================ END OF REPORTS ================

Produce the following. Be rigorous about attribution - every factual claim in your output must be tagged with the report(s) that support it, using the form [R1], [R2], [R3], and where reports conflict you must say so explicitly rather than silently picking one.

1. A single reconciled timeline from 01:52 to 03:13, minute by minute where the evidence supports it. Where two reports give different times for the same event, list both and state which you believe and why. Mark each entry with its source tag(s). Mark entries that are inferred rather than reported as [INFERRED] and justify the inference.
2. A table of every factual disagreement between the three reports. Columns: the claim, what each report says (or 'silent'), which is best supported by the evidence available, and what single piece of additional evidence would settle it definitively.
3. A causal chain. Distinguish trigger, vulnerability, and amplifiers. There are at least three contributing factors and no single root cause; say so and defend the decomposition. Explicitly evaluate and rule on SRE's claim that the deploy is a red herring.
4. An assessment of each of the three parties' self-serving bias. For each report, name at least one claim that is technically accurate but framed to shift responsibility, and explain the framing.
5. Adjudicate SRE action item (3), 'reduce per-pod pool size from 40 to 20'. Database Engineering objects to it. Decide who is right, using the connection arithmetic in the reports. Show the numbers: potential pooled connections, observed connections, and the count of out-of-pool sessions, and state whether they are consistent with each other. If the numbers in the three reports cannot all be true simultaneously, prove it.
6. A corrected action-item list of at most eight items, each with an owner (one of the three parties), a specific verifiable completion criterion, and a priority. Remove or rewrite any action item from the reports that would not have prevented or shortened this incident, and say which you removed and why.
7. State the three most important detection gaps, in the order you would fix them, with the specific alert definition (metric, threshold, window) for each.

prompts.title: Nine-version upgrade planning
prompts.text:
You maintain a service pinned to version 1.2.0 of the library below. Management wants it on 4.0.1. Here is the complete changelog between those points. Read it in full, then build the upgrade plan.

================ CHANGELOG: coldstream (a Java client library for a message broker) ================

## 4.0.1
- Fixed: `ConsumerGroup.rebalance()` could deadlock when `maxPollIntervalMs` was set below `sessionTimeoutMs`. The library now throws `IllegalConfigurationException` at construction time if this holds.
- Fixed: metrics tag `topic` was emitted as `topic_name` for exactly one metric, `coldstream.consumer.lag`. Now consistent. Dashboards referencing `topic_name` will break.

## 4.0.0 (BREAKING)
- REMOVED: `Producer.sendSync(Record)`. Use `Producer.send(Record).get()`. Deprecated since 3.0.0.
- REMOVED: the `coldstream.legacy.partitioner` system property and the `RoundRobinPartitioner` class. Deprecated since 2.4.0.
- CHANGED: `Consumer.poll(long timeoutMs)` now takes `java.time.Duration`. The long overload was deprecated in 3.2.0 and is now gone.
- CHANGED: default `enable.auto.commit` flipped from `true` to `false`. Applications that relied on the default now must commit explicitly or set it back.
- CHANGED: minimum Java version raised from 11 to 17.
- CHANGED: `Serializer<T>` and `Deserializer<T>` moved from `com.coldstream.serde` to `com.coldstream.api.serde`. A compatibility shim exists in `coldstream-compat` (a separate artifact) but it is deprecated on arrival and will be removed in 5.0.
- CHANGED: exception hierarchy reorganized. `ColdstreamException` is now checked; previously it extended `RuntimeException`. All `send`, `poll`, and `commit` methods now declare it.
- ADDED: `Producer.sendBatch(List<Record>)` with all-or-nothing semantics within a partition.
- ADDED: OpenTelemetry-native tracing. The old `TracingInterceptor` is deprecated.

## 3.6.2
- Fixed: a memory leak in `MetricsRegistry` when consumers were created and closed repeatedly (over 10,000 lifetimes).
- Fixed: `Consumer.seek()` on a partition not currently assigned silently did nothing; it now throws `IllegalStateException`.

## 3.6.0
- ADDED: `Consumer.pause(Collection<TopicPartition>)` and `resume`.
- ADDED: config `fetch.max.bytes.per.partition`, default 1 MiB.
- CHANGED: default `fetch.max.wait.ms` lowered from 500 to 100. This increases broker request rate roughly 3x for idle consumers. Set it back explicitly if your broker is request-rate constrained.
- DEPRECATED: `Consumer.assignment()` returning a mutable set. It now returns an unmodifiable set; mutating it throws.

## 3.4.0
- ADDED: transactional producer API: `beginTransaction`, `commitTransaction`, `abortTransaction`.
- CHANGED: `Record` is now immutable. `Record.setHeader()` removed (was added in 3.1.0, never announced as stable). Use `Record.toBuilder().header(...).build()`.
- Fixed: header values containing non-UTF-8 bytes were silently replaced with U+FFFD on serialization. They are now preserved. This changes the bytes on the wire for affected records.

## 3.2.0
- DEPRECATED: `Consumer.poll(long)` in favour of `Consumer.poll(Duration)`.
- ADDED: `ConsumerRebalanceListener.onPartitionsLost()` distinct from `onPartitionsRevoked()`. Applications that committed offsets in `onPartitionsRevoked` and relied on it being called on every revocation must now handle both. If you do not implement `onPartitionsLost`, the default implementation delegates to `onPartitionsRevoked`, which for a lost partition will attempt a commit that fails with `CommitFailedException`.
- CHANGED: `client.id` is now included in the consumer group protocol metadata. Brokers older than 2.8 reject the join request with `UNSUPPORTED_VERSION`.

## 3.0.0 (BREAKING)
- CHANGED: minimum Java version raised from 8 to 11.
- CHANGED: `Consumer.commitSync()` no longer retries internally. Previously it retried up to 5 times with a 100 ms backoff. Applications must now implement their own retry.
- CHANGED: the default `partitioner.class` changed from `RoundRobinPartitioner` to `StickyPartitioner`. For keyed records behaviour is unchanged; for null-keyed records, the distribution across partitions changes substantially and per-partition ordering guarantees are unaffected but downstream consumers assuming even distribution may be surprised.
- DEPRECATED: `Producer.sendSync(Record)`.
- REMOVED: `Consumer.subscribe(Pattern, ConsumerRebalanceListener, boolean)` four-arg overload.
- Fixed: `close()` on a producer with in-flight records could lose records if `linger.ms` was greater than 0. `close()` now flushes; `close(Duration.ZERO)` preserves the old behaviour.

## 2.8.0
- ADDED: `coldstream.security.protocol` supporting `SASL_SSL`.
- CHANGED: default `request.timeout.ms` raised from 30000 to 40000 to accommodate slower TLS handshakes.
- Fixed: consumer offsets could be committed for a partition after it was revoked, causing duplicate processing after a rebalance. This changes observable behaviour: applications that were silently double-processing will stop, which may surface latent idempotency bugs downstream.

## 2.4.0
- DEPRECATED: `RoundRobinPartitioner` and the `coldstream.legacy.partitioner` system property.
- ADDED: `Consumer.committed(Set<TopicPartition>)` batch variant; the single-partition variant now issues one request per call and is discouraged in loops.
- CHANGED: log output moved from `System.err` to SLF4J. Applications without an SLF4J binding on the classpath will see no library logs at all, silently.

## 2.0.0 (BREAKING)
- CHANGED: group coordination protocol upgraded. A consumer group cannot contain a mix of 1.x and 2.x clients; attempting it causes repeated rebalances with `INCONSISTENT_GROUP_PROTOCOL`. The documented procedure is to stop all consumers in the group, then start the new ones.
- CHANGED: `Deserializer.deserialize` signature gains a `Headers` parameter. All custom deserializers must be updated.
- REMOVED: `coldstream-shaded` artifact. Use `coldstream-core` plus explicit dependency management.
- CHANGED: default `auto.offset.reset` changed from `latest` to `earliest`. A new consumer group on an existing topic will now replay from the beginning.

## 1.4.0
- ADDED: `Consumer.endOffsets()`.
- Fixed: `Producer` could silently drop records when `buffer.memory` was exhausted and `max.block.ms` was 0. It now throws `BufferExhaustedException`.

## 1.2.0 (your current version)
- Baseline.

================ END CHANGELOG ================

Additional facts about the service you are upgrading:
- It runs on Java 11. It has 14 consumer instances in a single consumer group and 9 producer instances, all deployed from one artifact.
- It implements a custom `Deserializer<OrderEvent>` and a custom `Serializer<OrderEvent>`.
- It relies on auto-commit (it never calls commit explicitly).
- It calls `producer.sendSync(record)` in 41 places.
- It implements `ConsumerRebalanceListener.onPartitionsRevoked` and commits offsets there.
- It uses null-keyed records for one high-volume topic and its downstream analytics job assumes roughly even partition distribution.
- It sets `fetch.max.wait.ms` nowhere; the broker fleet is at 78% request-rate capacity at peak.
- It has no SLF4J binding on the classpath; logs currently appear on stderr and are collected.
- Brokers are on version 2.6.
- Its records include headers, some of which carry raw binary signatures that are not valid UTF-8.
- Downstream consumers of its output topic are not idempotent.

Deliverables:

1. A breaking-change matrix. One row per change in the changelog that affects this service, with columns: version introduced, change, which stated fact about the service makes it relevant, impact severity (blocker / behavioural / cosmetic), and required action. Include changes that are breaking for this service even though the changelog does not label them BREAKING - there are several, and finding them is the point.
2. An ordered upgrade plan with intermediate stops. Justify every intermediate version you stop at rather than jumping straight to 4.0.1, and state what you verify at each stop. At least one stop is forced by a coordination constraint rather than by a code change; identify it.
3. The 2.0.0 group-protocol change requires stopping all consumers. Reconcile that with the fact that the service must not be down. Give the concrete procedure, including what happens to the topic backlog during the stop and how long the stop can be, given a per-partition production rate you should state as an assumption.
4. Identify every change in this changelog that alters BEHAVIOUR without altering the API, such that a clean compile and a green unit-test run would not detect it. There are at least six. For each, describe the specific production symptom and the specific pre-deployment check that would catch it.
5. Three of the listed facts about the service interact to create a data-correctness hazard during the upgrade. Identify them, explain the interaction, and give the mitigation. (Hint: it involves offsets, a default change, and downstream idempotency.)
6. The broker version is 2.6. Find the changelog entry that makes this a hard blocker, quote it, and state what must happen first.
7. A rollback plan for each stop. State explicitly which steps are irreversible and why, and what you would do instead of rolling back for those.
8. Finally, a one-paragraph risk statement you would put at the top of the change request, naming the single highest-risk step and the evidence for that judgement.

prompts.title: Four meetings, one decision log
prompts.text:
Below are transcripts (lightly cleaned) of four meetings held over three weeks about the same project. Read all four, then produce the artefacts requested at the end. People change their minds between meetings and at least two decisions are silently reversed; catching that is the point of the exercise.

===== MEETING 1 - Tuesday, architecture kickoff, 50 min =====

PRIYA (eng lead): Purpose today is to decide the storage layer for the audit trail. Requirement from Legal is seven years retention, immutable, queryable by actor and by resource within five seconds for the last ninety days.
DEV: I'll say up front, I think this is a Postgres table with a BRIN index on timestamp and partitioning by month. We already run Postgres. Seven years at our volume is about 4 TB.
MARCUS (platform): 4 TB in the transactional cluster? That's a third of our current primary. I'd rather this not live next to checkout.
DEV: Separate cluster then. Same technology, separate blast radius.
PRIYA: Cost?
MARCUS: A dedicated 4 TB Postgres with a replica is roughly 1,900 a month all-in. Object storage with Parquet plus Athena-style querying would be maybe 120 a month for storage, plus per-query cost.
SOFIA (security): Immutability is my requirement. Postgres rows can be updated by anyone with the right grant. Object storage with versioning and an object-lock retention policy is genuinely immutable, enforced by the storage layer, not by our discipline.
DEV: We can revoke UPDATE and DELETE on the table.
SOFIA: From the application role, yes. Not from the superuser doing an incident recovery at 3 a.m.
PRIYA: What about the five-second query requirement?
MARCUS: Parquet on object storage, partitioned by day and by actor prefix, will hit five seconds for ninety days if the predicate is selective. If someone queries by resource without an actor, it's a full scan of ninety days, which is not five seconds.
DEV: So we need a secondary index, which object storage doesn't have.
PRIYA: Options?
MARCUS: Hybrid. Last ninety days in Postgres for query, everything in object storage for retention. Two systems, and you have to reconcile them.
SOFIA: I can accept ninety days of mutable Postgres if the object-storage copy is written synchronously and is the system of record for anything legal asks about.
PRIYA: Decision then: hybrid. Postgres for the ninety-day hot window, object storage with object-lock as the system of record. Marcus owns the write path. Dev owns the query API. Sofia signs off on the immutability configuration. Anyone object?
DEV: No, but I want it recorded that this is two systems and it will cost us in operational complexity.
PRIYA: Recorded. Next: schema. We'll take that Thursday.

===== MEETING 2 - Thursday, schema and write path, 45 min =====

MARCUS: Before schema, I need to revisit the write path. Synchronous write to object storage adds 40 to 90 milliseconds to every audited action. We audit every write in checkout. That's a p99 regression of about 90 ms on the checkout path, which blows our latency budget.
PRIYA: How much budget do we have?
MARCUS: Checkout p99 is 310 ms against a 400 ms SLO. So 90 ms takes us to 400. Zero margin.
DEV: Write to Postgres synchronously and to object storage asynchronously from a worker reading the Postgres table.
SOFIA: Then the system of record is the mutable one for some window. If the async worker is broken for an hour, an hour of audit records exist only in a mutable store.
DEV: We alert on worker lag.
SOFIA: Alerting is not a control. But I can live with it if the lag budget is small and enforced. What's small?
MARCUS: Sixty seconds, and we hard-fail writes if lag exceeds five minutes.
SOFIA: Hard-fail checkout because the audit worker is behind?
MARCUS: You said immutability was a hard requirement.
SOFIA: I said immutable retention. I did not say fail closed.
PRIYA: Let's not relitigate. Proposal: async write with a sixty-second target, alert at two minutes, page at five, and we do NOT fail checkout. Sofia, is that acceptable as a documented risk?
SOFIA: Acceptable with a documented risk and a quarterly review. Yes.
PRIYA: Decision recorded. Schema. Dev?
DEV: Columns: event_id ULID, occurred_at timestamptz, actor_type, actor_id, resource_type, resource_id, action, outcome, request_id, source_ip, payload jsonb, schema_version smallint.
SOFIA: payload jsonb concerns me. Free-form payload means PII lands in the audit trail and then it is immutable for seven years and we cannot honour a deletion request.
DEV: We can redact on write.
SOFIA: Redact based on what? A denylist you maintain by hand?
DEV: An allowlist of fields per action type.
SOFIA: Better. Who maintains it?
DEV: Whoever adds the action type. Enforced by a test that fails if an action type has no allowlist entry.
PRIYA: Good. Decision: payload is an allowlisted, per-action-type projection. Not free-form. Dev writes the enforcement test.
MARCUS: One more. ULID or UUIDv7 for event_id? ULID sorts lexically which is nice for object keys.
DEV: UUIDv7 sorts too and is standard. I'd take UUIDv7.
PRIYA: UUIDv7. Decided.

===== MEETING 3 - the following Wednesday, cost review with Finance, 30 min =====

FINANCE (R. Alder): I have a proposal here for 1,900 a month on a dedicated Postgres cluster plus object storage. Our infra budget for this quarter is already 6% over. Can this be one system?
MARCUS: The two-system design came out of a query-latency requirement and an immutability requirement.
FINANCE: Which requirement is negotiable?
PRIYA: Neither, formally. But let me check something. Sofia, if the ninety-day hot store were also object storage but with a proper index maintained by us, would that satisfy you?
SOFIA: I care about the seven-year copy. The hot store can be anything.
FINANCE: What if the hot store is the existing Postgres cluster rather than a dedicated one? Ninety days is what, 130 GB?
DEV: About 140 GB. That's fine on the existing primary, honestly.
MARCUS: I objected to that in the first meeting.
DEV: You objected to 4 TB. 140 GB with monthly partition drops is a different proposition.
MARCUS: ... that's fair. 140 GB I can live with, on a separate tablespace, and the partition-drop job has to be bulletproof because if it stops running we're back to 4 TB.
FINANCE: So we save the 1,900?
MARCUS: We save most of it. Object storage is 120. Call it 200 with request costs.
PRIYA: Decision: hot window on the EXISTING Postgres primary, separate tablespace, ninety-day retention by partition drop, with an alert if the drop job misses a cycle. This supersedes the dedicated-cluster decision from meeting one.
FINANCE: Thank you. When does this ship?
PRIYA: Six weeks.
DEV: Six weeks is the write path and the query API. The redaction allowlist for all forty-one existing action types is another two weeks.
PRIYA: Then eight. I'll update the roadmap.

===== MEETING 4 - Friday of that week, pre-implementation review, 55 min =====

PRIYA: Marcus has raised a concern by email. Marcus?
MARCUS: Partition drop on the existing primary. Dropping a 1.5 GB partition takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock briefly, and on our primary under peak load that has caused lock queues before. I want the drop to run in a maintenance window, which means the ninety-day window is really ninety-to-ninety-seven days depending on when the window falls.
SOFIA: That's fine. Ninety days is a floor, not a ceiling.
DEV: Then the query API needs to not promise exactly ninety days. It should return a coverage indicator.
PRIYA: Agreed, minor. Next?
DEV: Bigger issue. We decided async write from a worker reading the Postgres table. But if the hot store is now the shared primary, that worker is doing a full scan of the audit partition every few seconds looking for unshipped rows.
MARCUS: Add a shipped_at column and a partial index where shipped_at is null.
DEV: Then we're issuing UPDATEs against the audit table. Which Sofia will object to, because the audit table is supposed to be append-only.
SOFIA: I object to UPDATEs on the seven-year copy. The Postgres copy is a cache. Update it all you like.
DEV: In meeting two we said the Postgres copy is the system of record until the async worker ships it.
SOFIA: Then for that window it is the system of record and also mutable, which I already accepted as a documented risk. Adding a shipped_at update does not change the risk category.
PRIYA: Fine. shipped_at with a partial index. Decided.
MARCUS: Last thing. Object lock. I set the retention policy to seven years, compliance mode, which means nobody including the account root can delete an object before seven years elapse. If we write a bad object - say the redaction allowlist has a bug and PII lands in there - we cannot remove it for seven years.
SOFIA: That is the point of compliance mode.
MARCUS: I want governance mode with a break-glass role instead.
SOFIA: Governance mode means a sufficiently privileged principal can delete audit records, which defeats the control.
MARCUS: Compliance mode means a redaction bug becomes a seven-year regulatory exposure.
PRIYA: Sofia, what's your risk appetite here?
SOFIA: ... I'd take governance mode with the break-glass role restricted to a two-person quorum, alerting to my team on every use, and a quarterly access review. Not because I like it but because the redaction-bug scenario is real.
PRIYA: Decision: governance mode, two-person quorum break-glass, alert on use. Sofia documents the control. That's everything. Dev, start Monday.
DEV: One question - are we still on UUIDv7?
MARCUS: I'd rather ULID now that object keys matter more, since the hot store is not the system of record.
DEV: UUIDv7 also sorts. It's the same property.
MARCUS: ULID is 26 characters base32, no dashes, better as an object key prefix.
PRIYA: Not worth the meeting time. Dev, your call, write it down.
DEV: UUIDv7.

===== END OF TRANSCRIPTS =====

Produce:

1. A DECISION LOG. One row per decision with: decision ID, the decision as a single declarative sentence, the meeting where it was made, the owner, the status (STANDS / SUPERSEDED / REVERSED / UNRESOLVED), and if superseded or reversed, the decision ID that replaced it and the meeting where that happened. There are at least two silent reversals and at least one decision that was never actually closed - find them.
2. A CONTRADICTION TABLE. Every place where two statements across the four meetings are in tension. Give both quotations (attributed to speaker and meeting), state whether the contradiction was resolved and where, and if unresolved, state what needs to happen.
3. A REQUIREMENTS TRACE. List the three original requirements stated in meeting 1, and for each one, state whether the final design satisfies it, partially satisfies it, or violates it, citing the specific meeting and speaker for the evidence. One of the three is arguably violated by the final design; identify it and argue both sides before ruling.
4. An OPEN QUESTIONS list, each with the person best placed to answer and why it is still open.
5. A RISK REGISTER of at least six risks introduced by the decisions, each with: description, the decision that introduced it, likelihood, impact, the mitigation that was agreed (or 'none agreed'), and the residual risk.
6. Marcus's position changes materially between meeting 1 and meeting 3. Quote both positions, explain what new information changed his mind, and assess whether the change was justified by the new information or whether he was overruled by budget pressure. Be specific about which.
7. A one-page implementation brief for the engineer starting Monday, containing only decisions that STAND, written as unambiguous instructions, with every ambiguity from the transcripts either resolved by you (with justification) or flagged as blocking.
8. Finally: estimate the schedule. Priya said six weeks, then eight. Based on the scope changes across the four meetings, state whether eight weeks is defensible, list the scope that was added AFTER the estimate was given, and give your own estimate with the reasoning.

prompts.title: Spec versus implementation adjudication
prompts.text:
You are the API owner. A customer has filed a bug. Below you have the relevant part of the published API specification, the customer's bug report, an internal support thread, and a fragment of the actual server behaviour captured from logs. Decide who is right.

================ 1. PUBLISHED SPECIFICATION, section 6: Partial Updates ================

6.1 The PATCH method

The PATCH method applies a partial modification to a resource. The request body MUST be a JSON object whose keys are a subset of the writable fields of the resource. Keys not present in the request body are left unmodified.

6.2 Null semantics

A field explicitly set to null in a PATCH body clears that field, setting it to its zero value (empty string for strings, empty array for arrays, null for nullable references). A field ABSENT from the PATCH body is left unmodified. Clients MUST distinguish between absent and null.

6.3 Nested objects

When a writable field is itself an object, PATCH semantics apply recursively: keys present in the nested object are updated, keys absent are preserved. To replace a nested object wholesale, clients SHOULD use PUT on the nested resource where one is exposed, or set the parent field to null and then PATCH the desired contents in a second request.

6.4 Arrays

Arrays are replaced wholesale. There is no element-level merge. An empty array clears the field. Note that this differs from the treatment of nested objects described in 6.3.

6.5 Concurrency

PATCH requests SHOULD include an If-Match header carrying the resource's current ETag. If If-Match is present and does not match, the server returns 412 Precondition Failed and applies no changes. If If-Match is absent, the server applies the update unconditionally (last-write-wins).

6.6 Validation
