The merged resource - that is, the existing resource with the patch applied - MUST satisfy all resource-level invariants. Validation errors return 422 with a body listing each violated constraint and a JSON Pointer to the offending location IN THE MERGED DOCUMENT.

6.7 Atomicity

A PATCH request is atomic: either all changes in the body are applied or none are.

6.8 Idempotency

PATCH is not guaranteed idempotent in general. However, a PATCH body containing only literal values (no relative operations such as increments) applied twice in succession, with no intervening writes, MUST produce the same final resource state as applying it once.

6.9 Response

On success the server returns 200 with the complete updated resource representation and a new ETag. Servers MAY return 204 with no body if the client sends `Prefer: return=minimal`.

================ 2. CUSTOMER BUG REPORT (ticket SUP-88213) ================

Title: PATCH on /v2/subscriptions clears fields I did not send
Reported by: Hana Ito, integration engineer at Wexford Logistics
Severity claimed: high, blocking our go-live

Description:
We are updating a subscription's billing contact. Our PATCH body is:

  { "billing": { "contact": { "email": "ops@wexford.example" } } }

The subscription before the request:

  { "id": "sub_8812", "plan": "growth", "seats": 40,
    "billing": { "currency": "EUR", "po_number": "WX-2231",
                 "contact": { "name": "Hana Ito", "email": "hana@wexford.example", "phone": "+353-1-555-0134" } },
    "tags": ["eu", "logistics"], "trial_ends_at": "2026-02-01T00:00:00Z" }

The subscription after the request:

  { "id": "sub_8812", "plan": "growth", "seats": 40,
    "billing": { "currency": "EUR", "po_number": null,
                 "contact": { "name": null, "email": "ops@wexford.example", "phone": null } },
    "tags": [], "trial_ends_at": "2026-02-01T00:00:00Z" }

We lost po_number, contact.name, contact.phone and our tags. Section 6.3 of your spec says absent keys in a nested object are preserved. This is clearly a bug. We have 3,400 subscriptions to migrate and we cannot proceed.

Additional note: when we retried the same request a second time we got a 422 saying `/billing/contact/name` must not be empty. So the first request produced a resource that your own validation rejects. That seems to violate section 6.6.

================ 3. INTERNAL SUPPORT THREAD ================

[Support, J. Baptiste] Reproduced. Confirmed we clear nested absent keys. Escalating to API team.

[API team, L. Marchetti] This is not a bug, it is a documented behaviour change. See release note for v2.9: 'PATCH now uses replace semantics for nested objects to align with RFC 7396 merge-patch. Clients relying on recursive preservation must send the full nested object.' We shipped that eleven weeks ago.

[Support, J. Baptiste] Section 6.3 of the published spec still says recursive preservation. Is the spec stale?

[API team, L. Marchetti] The spec page is generated from the v2.8 branch. There is a ticket to regenerate it. DOC-1190, open since v2.9 shipped.

[Platform, A. Duarte] Hold on. RFC 7396 merge-patch does NOT have replace semantics for nested objects. Merge-patch is recursive for objects - absent keys are preserved, and null deletes the key. What we shipped is neither our old behaviour nor merge-patch. Can someone show me the diff?

[API team, L. Marchetti] The change was to deserialize the patch body into the resource DTO and then persist the DTO. Fields absent from the JSON deserialize to their type defaults, and we persist those defaults.

[Platform, A. Duarte] That is not a semantics decision, that is a deserialization accident. And it explains the tags clearing too - the customer did not send tags at all, and the array field defaulted to empty.

[Support, J. Baptiste] The customer also reports a 422 on retry. If the first PATCH produced a state that fails validation, then either validation is not running on PATCH or it is running against the patch body rather than the merged document.

[API team, L. Marchetti] Validation runs on the DTO before persist. The DTO after deserialization has name = null, and the not-empty constraint is only checked when the field is present in the incoming JSON. On the retry, name is present in the stored entity as null and the loaded-then-validated path checks it. Different code paths.

[Platform, A. Duarte] So we have three defects, not one. And one of them corrupted 3,400 customer records' worth of data if they run their migration.

[Legal/Compliance, no name] If po_number is being cleared on EU subscriptions and that field feeds invoicing, we have an invoicing-accuracy problem, not just an API problem. Please quantify how many customers are affected.

================ 4. CAPTURED SERVER BEHAVIOUR (5 requests, anonymized) ================

R1  PATCH /v2/subscriptions/sub_0001  body {"seats": 55}  no If-Match
    before: seats 40, tags ["a","b"], billing.po_number "P-1"
    after:  seats 55, tags [], billing.po_number null      -> 200

R2  PATCH /v2/subscriptions/sub_0002  body {"seats": 55, "tags": ["a","b"], "billing": {"currency":"EUR","po_number":"P-2","contact":{"name":"X","email":"x@e.example","phone":"+1"}}}
    before: seats 40 ... (as stored)
    after:  seats 55, everything else identical to what was sent  -> 200

R3  PATCH /v2/subscriptions/sub_0003  body {"billing": {"contact": {"email": null}}}  If-Match "W/\"v7\""
    stored ETag was W/"v7"
    after:  billing.contact.email "", name null, phone null, po_number null, currency null, tags []  -> 200

R4  PATCH /v2/subscriptions/sub_0004  body {"seats": 0}
    after:  seats 0, and a 422 was NOT returned even though the resource invariant says seats >= 1  -> 200

R5  PATCH /v2/subscriptions/sub_0005  body {"seats": -3}
    -> 422 with body {"errors":[{"pointer":"/seats","detail":"must be >= 1"}]}

================ END OF MATERIALS ================

Adjudicate. Your output must include:

1. A verdict on the customer's primary complaint: spec bug, implementation bug, or both. Justify by citing the specific spec section and the specific evidence, and state clearly which document is authoritative and why.
2. An enumerated defect list. There are at least four distinct defects visible in these materials, and they are in different layers. For each: a title, the layer (specification / deserialization / validation / documentation / process), the exact evidence (quote the section, ticket line, or request number), and the observable customer impact.
3. A precise statement of what the CURRENT implemented semantics actually are, derived from R1 through R5. Write it as a rule set that would let someone predict the outcome of any PATCH. Then contrast it, point by point, with (a) the published spec section 6, and (b) genuine RFC 7396 merge-patch. Produce a three-column comparison table covering: absent scalar, null scalar, absent nested object, absent key within a present nested object, absent array, empty array, and null array.
4. Explain R4 versus R5. Both send an out-of-range seats value in the customer's mental model, but only one is rejected. Give the precise reason from the evidence in the support thread, and state what this implies about where validation runs.
5. Explain R3 in full. It clears more than the other requests. Say exactly why, and note the one thing about R3 that is consistent with the spec.
6. A remediation plan with three horizons: what you ship in 24 hours, what you ship in two weeks, and what you change structurally. Include the data-repair question: can the cleared po_number values be recovered, what would you need, and what do you tell the customer if they cannot?
7. The customer communication. Write the actual reply to Hana Ito: acknowledge, state what is broken in plain terms, state what she should do RIGHT NOW to unblock her 3,400-record migration safely, and state what you will do and by when. Do not blame her. Do not promise anything the evidence does not support.
8. Finally, one process defect is the underlying cause of most of this. Name it, cite the line in the support thread that reveals it, and give the control that prevents recurrence.

prompts.title: Two vendor contracts compared
prompts.text:
Procurement has shortlisted two managed streaming vendors. The relevant contract excerpts are reproduced in full below. Read both, then produce the analysis requested at the end. Every conclusion must cite the clause number and the vendor.

================ VENDOR A: NIMBUS STREAMS - MASTER SERVICES AGREEMENT (excerpts) ================

2. SERVICE LEVELS
2.1 Nimbus will use commercially reasonable efforts to make the Service Available at least 99.95% of the time during each calendar month.
2.2 'Available' means the Service accepts and acknowledges a well-formed produce request and returns a response with a status other than 5xx. Latency is not a component of Availability.
2.3 'Monthly Uptime Percentage' is calculated as (total minutes in the month minus Unavailable Minutes) divided by total minutes in the month. A minute is an Unavailable Minute only if ALL produce requests issued by Customer during that minute fail. Minutes in which no request was issued are treated as Available.
2.4 Availability is measured per Region. A multi-Region deployment is deemed Available if any one Region is Available.

3. SERVICE CREDITS
3.1 If Monthly Uptime Percentage falls below 99.95% but is at least 99.0%, Customer is eligible for a credit of 10% of the monthly fee for the affected Region.
3.2 If Monthly Uptime Percentage falls below 99.0% but is at least 95.0%, the credit is 25%.
3.3 Below 95.0%, the credit is 50%.
3.4 Credits are the sole and exclusive remedy for any failure to meet Service Levels.
3.5 To receive a credit, Customer must submit a claim within fifteen (15) days of the end of the affected month, including Customer-side logs demonstrating the failed requests. Claims submitted without such logs will be rejected.
3.6 Credits are applied against future invoices and are not refundable in cash. Unused credits expire twelve (12) months after issuance and upon termination for any reason.

4. EXCLUSIONS
4.1 The Service Levels do not apply to unavailability caused by: (a) factors outside Nimbus's reasonable control, including any force majeure event or Internet access problems beyond Nimbus's demarcation point; (b) Customer's software, hardware, or third-party services; (c) Customer's exceeding of documented quotas or rate limits; (d) scheduled maintenance as described in 4.2; (e) beta, preview, or 'Early Access' features; (f) suspension of Customer's account under Section 9.
4.2 Nimbus may perform scheduled maintenance for up to eight (8) hours per calendar month with at least forty-eight (48) hours' notice. Scheduled maintenance minutes are excluded from Unavailable Minutes.
4.3 Emergency maintenance may be performed without notice and is likewise excluded.

5. DATA AND PORTABILITY
5.1 Customer retains all right, title and interest in Customer Data.
5.2 Upon termination, Nimbus will retain Customer Data for thirty (30) days, during which Customer may export it using the Service's standard export API.
5.3 The standard export API is rate limited to 200 MB per minute per account. Nimbus offers a bulk export service at an additional charge of USD 0.09 per GB.
5.4 Nimbus makes no commitment regarding the format of exported data beyond that it will be machine readable.

6. SECURITY
6.1 Nimbus maintains SOC 2 Type II certification and will provide the report annually under NDA.
6.2 Nimbus encrypts Customer Data at rest using AES-256 and in transit using TLS 1.2 or higher.
6.3 Nimbus will notify Customer of a Security Incident affecting Customer Data without undue delay and in any event within seventy-two (72) hours of confirmation.
6.4 Customer-managed encryption keys are available on the Enterprise tier at an additional 15% of the monthly fee.

7. LIABILITY
7.1 Neither party's aggregate liability shall exceed the fees paid by Customer in the twelve (12) months preceding the claim.
7.2 Neither party is liable for indirect, incidental, special, consequential or punitive damages, including loss of data, loss of profits, or loss of business.
7.3 The limitations in 7.1 and 7.2 do not apply to breaches of confidentiality or to a party's indemnification obligations.

8. TERM AND TERMINATION
8.1 Initial term of thirty-six (36) months, automatically renewing for successive twelve (12) month terms unless either party gives ninety (90) days' notice.
8.2 Customer may terminate for convenience at any time upon ninety (90) days' notice, subject to payment of the remaining committed spend for the then-current term.
8.3 Either party may terminate for material breach not cured within thirty (30) days of written notice.

9. PRICING
9.1 Committed spend of USD 42,000 per month for thirty-six months. Usage above the commitment is billed at list rates.
9.2 List rates: USD 0.11 per GB ingested, USD 0.04 per GB egressed, USD 0.021 per partition-hour.
9.3 Annual price increases capped at the lesser of 7% or CPI plus 3%.

================ VENDOR B: HALCYON DATA - SUBSCRIPTION AGREEMENT (excerpts) ================

A. AVAILABILITY COMMITMENT
A.1 Halcyon commits to 99.9% Monthly Availability for the Production Tier.
A.2 'Availability' is measured by Halcyon's synthetic probe, which issues one produce and one consume request per minute from three independent network vantage points. A minute is Unavailable if two or more vantage points report failure OR if end-to-end probe latency exceeds 2,000 ms at two or more vantage points.
A.3 Availability is measured across the entire account, aggregated over all Regions. A Region-specific outage that leaves the account-level probe succeeding does not count as Unavailable.
A.4 Halcyon publishes measured Availability monthly on its status page. Customer may rely on the published figure without submitting logs.

B. REMEDIES
B.1 Below 99.9% and at or above 99.5%: credit of 15% of the monthly subscription fee.
B.2 Below 99.5% and at or above 99.0%: credit of 30%.
B.3 Below 99.0%: credit of 100% of the monthly subscription fee for that month.
B.4 If Availability is below 99.0% in any three months within a rolling twelve-month period, Customer may terminate for cause with no early-termination charge and receive a pro-rata refund of prepaid fees.
B.5 Credits are automatically applied; no claim is required.

C. EXCLUSIONS
C.1 Excluded: force majeure; Customer's breach of the Acceptable Use Policy; Customer exceeding provisioned throughput by more than 10% for more than five consecutive minutes.
C.2 Halcyon performs maintenance without a stated cap on duration, but maintenance windows count toward Unavailable Minutes if the Service is not Available during them. Halcyon commits to seventy-two (72) hours' notice for planned maintenance affecting availability.
C.3 There is no exclusion for beta features because Halcyon does not offer beta features under this Agreement.

D. DATA AND PORTABILITY
D.1 Upon termination or expiry, Halcyon will provide a full export of Customer Data in Apache Parquet or newline-delimited JSON, at Customer's election, at no charge, within ten (10) business days.
D.2 Halcyon will retain Customer Data for ninety (90) days post-termination unless Customer requests earlier deletion.
D.3 Halcyon will provide a written certificate of deletion within thirty (30) days of Customer's deletion request.

E. SECURITY
E.1 Halcyon maintains ISO 27001 certification. SOC 2 Type II is 'in progress' with an expected completion date noted in Exhibit 3.
E.2 Encryption at rest uses AES-256 with Halcyon-managed keys. Customer-managed keys are on the roadmap for the second half of next year.
E.3 Halcyon will notify Customer of a Security Incident within twenty-four (24) hours of detection.
E.4 Halcyon subcontracts storage to a third-party hyperscaler listed in Exhibit 4 and remains responsible for its subprocessors' performance.

F. LIABILITY
F.1 Halcyon's aggregate liability shall not exceed the greater of USD 250,000 or the fees paid in the preceding six (6) months.
F.2 Exclusion of indirect and consequential damages, mutual.
F.3 Data loss caused by Halcyon's gross negligence is carved out of F.2 but remains subject to the cap in F.1.

G. TERM
G.1 Initial term of twelve (12) months, renewing monthly thereafter.
G.2 Either party may terminate for convenience on thirty (30) days' notice after the initial term.
G.3 Price is fixed for the initial term; thereafter Halcyon may change prices on sixty (60) days' notice.

H. PRICING
H.1 USD 51,500 per month, all-inclusive of the provisioned throughput stated in Exhibit 1 (1.4 GB/s ingest, 4.2 GB/s egress).
H.2 Overage above provisioned throughput is billed at USD 0.14 per GB ingested and USD 0.05 per GB egressed.
H.3 No committed-spend requirement.

================ OUR SITUATION ================
We ingest 780 GB/day and egress 2,900 GB/day, growing 4% month over month. We run in two regions. Our own product SLA to our customers is 99.9% monthly with financial penalties of USD 40,000 per 0.1% below target. A total outage of our streaming layer takes our product down. Our security review requires customer-managed keys within nine months and SOC 2 Type II from all tier-1 vendors. Our finance team plans on a three-year horizon.

================ END OF MATERIALS ================

Deliver:

1. A clause-by-clause comparison table across at least ten dimensions (availability definition, measurement method, credit structure, exclusions, maintenance treatment, data portability, security posture, liability cap, term flexibility, price). Cite clause identifiers for every cell.
2. Effective availability analysis. The two definitions of 'Available' are not comparable. Explain precisely why Vendor A's 99.95% may be WEAKER in practice than Vendor B's 99.9%, using clauses A.2, 2.2, 2.3 and 2.4. Construct a concrete 60-minute outage scenario, with numbers, in which Vendor A owes zero credits and Vendor B owes a 30% credit for exactly the same real-world customer impact. Show the minute-by-minute accounting.
3. Compute the annual cost of each vendor at our current volume and at our volume 24 months from now at 4% monthly growth. Show the arithmetic including overage. For Vendor A use the committed spend plus overage at list rates; for Vendor B use the flat fee plus overage above provisioned throughput (state whether our current volume exceeds the provisioned throughput and show the conversion from GB/day to GB/s).
4. Risk-adjusted comparison against OUR customer SLA. If a vendor outage causes us to breach our own 99.9% SLA, what do we actually recover? Compute, for a hypothetical month with 5 hours of total vendor outage: our penalty exposure, the credit each vendor would owe, and the net position. Do this for both vendors and state the shortfall in dollars.
5. Identify at least eight asymmetries or traps that a casual reader would miss. Examples of the kind of thing to look for: which credit expires, which requires evidence you may not have, whose measurement you cannot audit, which cap is lower in absolute terms at our spend level, which exclusion swallows the commitment. For each, cite the clause and quantify where possible.
6. Blocking issues against our stated requirements. Go through the four requirements in 'OUR SITUATION' and rule each vendor pass/fail/conditional, citing clauses. One vendor fails a hard requirement outright; identify it.
7. Negotiation list. For each vendor, the five clause changes you would demand, in priority order, with the specific redline language you want and what you would concede to get it. Be realistic about which asks are winnable.
8. A recommendation of at most 200 words, naming a vendor, the two clauses that decided it, and the single condition under which you would reverse the recommendation.

prompts.title: Design doc versus review thread
prompts.text:
A design document and the code review thread for its implementation are below. They do not agree. Reconcile them and produce the outputs listed at the end.

================ DOCUMENT 1: DESIGN DOC, 'Ledger Snapshot Compaction', v4, approved ================

Authors: E. Brandt, N. Kaur. Reviewers: three approvals recorded.

Background
The event store holds 41 billion ledger events. Rebuilding an account's balance requires replaying every event for that account, which for our largest accounts is 6.1 million events and takes 94 seconds. We need sub-second balance reads.

Goals
G1. p99 balance read under 200 ms for any account.
G2. Snapshots must never produce a balance different from a full replay. This is a correctness requirement, not a performance one.
G3. Compaction must not increase steady-state write latency by more than 5 ms at p99.
G4. The system must tolerate a compaction job crashing at any point without producing an incorrect snapshot.

Non-goals
N1. We are not changing the event schema.
N2. We are not addressing cross-account invariants in this document.

Design
Every account has a snapshot record: (account_id, up_to_sequence, balance_cents, currency, computed_at, snapshot_version). A balance read loads the snapshot and replays only events with sequence greater than up_to_sequence.

Snapshots are produced by a compaction job that runs every 15 minutes. For each account with more than 5,000 events since its last snapshot, the job reads the snapshot, replays forward, and writes a new snapshot row with a higher up_to_sequence. Snapshot writes are idempotent: writing a snapshot with an up_to_sequence less than or equal to the stored one is a no-op.

Ordering. Events for an account are totally ordered by a per-account monotonic sequence number assigned at append time using a database sequence per account shard. Sequence numbers are dense (no gaps) within an account.

Correctness argument for G2. Because sequence numbers are dense and totally ordered per account, and because a snapshot records the exact sequence up to which events were folded, replaying events strictly greater than up_to_sequence reproduces the full fold. Snapshot writes are conditional on the stored up_to_sequence being lower, so a crashed job leaves either the old snapshot or a complete new one.

Schema versioning. snapshot_version records the version of the fold function. A reader that encounters a snapshot_version higher than it understands must ignore the snapshot and replay from zero. A reader encountering a lower version may use the snapshot.

Rollout. Shadow mode for two weeks comparing snapshot-derived balances against full replay for 1% of reads, alerting on any mismatch. Then progressive enablement.

Capacity. 41 billion events, 180 million accounts, snapshot row 96 bytes, so about 17 GB of snapshot data. Compaction reads roughly 2% of events per cycle.

================ DOCUMENT 2: CODE REVIEW THREAD on PR #2288, 'ledger: snapshot compaction' ================

[reviewer: t.oyelaran] Line 141: you are reading the snapshot and the events in two separate queries without a transaction or a consistent read timestamp. Between the two reads a concurrent append can insert an event with sequence <= up_to_sequence of a snapshot written by another compaction worker. Have you thought about this?

[author: e.brandt] Sequences are assigned at append time and are monotonic, so an event with a lower sequence cannot appear after a higher one has been committed.

[reviewer: t.oyelaran] Assigned monotonically, yes. COMMITTED monotonically, no. We use a database sequence, and sequence values are handed out before commit. Transaction A can take sequence 100, transaction B take 101, B commits, A commits later. A reader between the two commits sees 101 but not 100. Your dense-sequence assumption in the design doc is false under concurrency.

[author: e.brandt] That is a real problem. In practice the window is milliseconds.

[reviewer: t.oyelaran] The compaction job runs for 40 minutes across 180 million accounts. Milliseconds times a lot of accounts is a certainty, not a possibility.

[reviewer: m.solberg] Separate issue. Line 208: the fold function switches on event_type with a default branch that logs and skips unknown types. If we add an event type and an old compaction worker is still running during a deploy, it will produce a snapshot that silently omits those events, and then the snapshot is authoritative. That violates G2.

[author: n.kaur] The snapshot_version field handles that.

[reviewer: m.solberg] Only if you bump it, and only if the READER rejects it. The design doc says a reader encountering a LOWER version may use the snapshot. So an old snapshot written by an old worker with a lower version will be trusted by a new reader. That is exactly the failure case.

[author: n.kaur] Then the rule should be that readers only trust snapshots whose version equals theirs.

[reviewer: m.solberg] Which means every deploy invalidates every snapshot and we replay 41 billion events. That is not viable either.

[reviewer: t.oyelaran] Line 302: the shadow comparison samples 1% of reads. Our largest accounts are 0.0004% of accounts but 30% of read volume. A 1% uniform sample of READS is fine; a 1% sample of ACCOUNTS would not be. Which is it in the code? Looks like accounts to me.

[author: e.brandt] It samples accounts. I'll change it.

[reviewer: p.iyer] Line 77: compaction writes use a conditional update 'WHERE up_to_sequence < :new'. That is correct for idempotency but it is not correct for the crash case the doc claims. If the job crashes after computing the balance but the balance was computed from a partial read - see t.oyelaran's point - the write still succeeds because the sequence went up. Idempotency is not the same as atomicity with respect to the read.

[reviewer: p.iyer] Also: currency. The snapshot has a single balance_cents and a currency, but line 190 folds events without checking that all events for an account share a currency. Is that guaranteed? The design doc does not say.

[author: n.kaur] It is guaranteed by the account creation path. Accounts are single-currency.

[reviewer: p.iyer] Then the fold should assert it rather than assume it, because if it is ever violated the snapshot silently produces a wrong number and G2 says never.

[reviewer: t.oyelaran] One more. The doc says compaction runs every 15 minutes and reads 2% of events per cycle. 2% of 41 billion is 820 million events per cycle, in 15 minutes, which is 911,000 events per second sustained. What is the actual measured throughput?

[author: e.brandt] Current measured throughput on the staging fleet is about 140,000 events per second with 24 workers.

[reviewer: t.oyelaran] So a cycle takes 97 minutes, not 15. Either the cadence or the capacity number in the doc is wrong.

[reviewer: m.solberg] Approving with comments is not appropriate here. I am requesting changes.

[author: e.brandt] Understood. Let me collect the issues.

================ END OF MATERIALS ================

Produce the following:

1. A reconciled issue list. For each issue raised in the review, state: which design-doc goal or claim it contradicts (quote the doc), whether it is a doc defect, a code defect, or both, its severity with respect to G1-G4, and whether it was resolved in the thread, partially resolved, or left open.
2. The design doc contains a correctness argument that is unsound. Quote it, state the precise false premise, and explain the failure with a concrete interleaving: two transactions, their sequence numbers, their commit order, the compaction read, and the resulting incorrect snapshot. Give exact numbers.
3. The snapshot_version rule in the doc is self-defeating: as m.solberg observes, one reading forces incorrect snapshots to be trusted and the other forces a full replay of the corpus on every deploy. Design a third rule that avoids both horns. State it precisely, explain how it handles the unknown-event-type case, and explain what it costs.
4. Adjudicate the capacity dispute. Recompute the numbers yourself from the doc's own figures (41 billion events, 2% per cycle, 15-minute cadence) and from the measured 140,000 events/second. State the required worker count for a 15-minute cycle at the measured per-worker rate, and state which of the doc's numbers you believe is wrong and why. Then propose a cadence and worker count that is actually achievable and check it against G3.
5. The sampling issue is subtler than it looks. Explain why sampling accounts versus sampling reads changes what the shadow-mode alert can detect, given that large accounts dominate read volume but are a vanishing fraction of accounts. Then specify the sampling scheme you would implement, including how you guarantee that every account above a size threshold is compared at least once per day, and compute the extra read load that imposes.
6. Rewrite the doc's 'Correctness argument for G2' section so that it is actually sound given everything in the review thread. It must address commit-order versus assignment-order, the read consistency of the compaction job, the unknown-event-type case, and the currency assumption. Write it as it would appear in v5 of the document.
7. A list of the changes required to PR #2288, ordered so that a reviewer could check them off, each with the line number from the thread where applicable and an acceptance criterion.
8. Finally, one issue that NOBODY in the thread raised but that follows from the materials. State it, justify it from the documents, and say how you would test for it.

prompts.title: Retention policy compliance gaps
prompts.text:
Three governing documents are reproduced below. They were written by different teams and they conflict. Read all three, then perform the gap analysis described at the end. Cite document and section for every finding.

================ DOC A: CORPORATE DATA RETENTION POLICY, v6.2 ================

1. Scope
This Policy applies to all Personal Data and Business Records processed by the Company and its subsidiaries, in all systems, including backups, logs, analytics stores, and third-party processors.

2. Definitions
2.1 'Personal Data' means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person.
2.2 'Pseudonymised Data' means Personal Data processed such that it can no longer be attributed to a specific person without the use of additional information, where that additional information is kept separately and subject to technical measures.
2.3 'Anonymised Data' means data that is not Personal Data because re-identification is not reasonably possible. Anonymised Data is out of scope of this Policy.
2.4 'Business Record' means data required for financial, tax, or contractual purposes.

3. Retention Schedule
3.1 Customer account records: retained for the duration of the customer relationship plus twenty-four (24) months.
3.2 Transaction records: seven (7) years from the transaction date, as a Business Record.
3.3 Application logs containing Personal Data: ninety (90) days.
3.4 Application logs not containing Personal Data: eighteen (18) months.
3.5 Security and audit logs: twenty-four (24) months. Where a security log contains Personal Data, the Personal Data elements must be pseudonymised after ninety (90) days.
3.6 Analytics event data: thirteen (13) months in identified form, indefinitely in aggregated form.
3.7 Support tickets and correspondence: thirty-six (36) months after ticket closure.
3.8 Marketing contact data: until consent is withdrawn, or twenty-four (24) months of inactivity, whichever is sooner.
3.9 Backups: backups are retained for thirty-five (35) days on a rolling basis. Data deleted from primary systems will persist in backups until the backup expires. This is deemed acceptable.

4. Deletion Requests
4.1 Upon a valid erasure request from a Data Subject, the Company will delete Personal Data relating to that Data Subject within thirty (30) days.
4.2 Data that must be retained as a Business Record under 3.2 is exempt from erasure. The Company will retain the minimum necessary fields.
4.3 The Company will instruct third-party processors to delete within the same window.
4.4 Deletion from backups is not performed; see 3.9.

5. Enforcement
5.1 Each system owner is responsible for implementing the schedule for their system.
5.2 The Data Protection Officer conducts an annual review.
5.3 Exceptions require written approval from the DPO and are recorded in the Exception Register.

================ DOC B: EXCERPT, REGULATION 'DPA-2029' (applicable in our primary market) ================

Article 12 - Storage limitation
(1) Personal Data shall be kept in a form which permits identification of Data Subjects for no longer than is necessary for the purposes for which the Personal Data are processed.
(2) A controller relying on a legal obligation to retain data beyond the period in paragraph (1) shall document the specific legal provision imposing that obligation and shall restrict processing of such data to the purpose of that obligation.

Article 17 - Right to erasure
(1) The Data Subject shall have the right to obtain erasure of Personal Data concerning them without undue delay and in any event within one (1) month of the request.
(2) The period in paragraph (1) may be extended by two (2) further months where necessary, taking into account the complexity of the request, provided the controller informs the Data Subject of the extension and the reasons for it within one month of the request.
(3) Erasure obligations extend to all copies, including copies held by processors and copies held in backup media. Where immediate erasure from backup media is technically infeasible, the controller shall (a) place the data beyond use, (b) document the technical infeasibility, and (c) ensure erasure occurs upon the next restoration or expiry of the backup, whichever is sooner.
(4) The right does not apply to the extent processing is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation, for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims, or for archiving purposes in the public interest.

Article 21 - Pseudonymisation
(1) Pseudonymised Data remains Personal Data for the purposes of this Regulation.
(2) A controller that pseudonymises data in order to satisfy a storage limitation shall demonstrate that the additional information enabling re-identification is subject to separate storage and to access controls at least as strong as those applied to the original data.

Article 30 - Records of processing
(1) Controllers shall maintain a record of processing activities including, for each category of Personal Data, the envisaged time limits for erasure.
(2) Where a controller cannot state a specific time limit, it shall state the criteria used to determine the period.

Article 34 - Breach notification
(1) A personal data breach shall be notified to the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than seventy-two (72) hours after the controller becomes aware of it.
(2) Where the breach is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller shall communicate the breach to the affected Data Subjects without undue delay.

Article 41 - Financial records exception
(1) Nothing in this Regulation requires the erasure of records that a controller is required to retain under applicable accounting or tax law. Such retention shall not exceed the period specified by that law by more than twelve (12) months.

================ DOC C: ENGINEERING RUNBOOK, 'Data Deletion Procedures', last updated 14 months ago ================

RB-1. Scope
This runbook covers the operational steps for handling a Data Subject erasure request (DSR-Delete) and for scheduled retention enforcement.

RB-2. Systems in scope
  - accounts-db (PostgreSQL, primary customer records)
  - txn-store (PostgreSQL, transactions)
  - eventlake (object storage, analytics events in Parquet)
  - searchidx (Elasticsearch, denormalized customer search index)
  - supportdesk (third-party SaaS, tickets)
  - mailer (third-party SaaS, marketing)
  - logs-hot (Elasticsearch, 30 days), logs-cold (object storage, 18 months)
  - metrics (time-series DB, 400 days)
  - datawarehouse (columnar, all of the above ETL'd nightly)

RB-3. DSR-Delete procedure
  Step 1. Ops receives the ticket and verifies identity. SLA: 3 business days.
  Step 2. Run `dsr-tool delete --subject <id>`. This tool covers accounts-db, txn-store (soft delete only), searchidx, and mailer.
  Step 3. File a manual ticket with the supportdesk vendor. Their stated turnaround is 45 days.
  Step 4. eventlake is not covered by dsr-tool. Analytics events are considered pseudonymised because they key on a hashed user id. No action required.
  Step 5. logs-hot and logs-cold are not covered. They expire naturally.
  Step 6. datawarehouse is refreshed nightly from sources; deletions propagate on the next ETL run. Note: the ETL is incremental and does not process deletions; a full refresh runs quarterly.
  Step 7. metrics contains no personal data.
  Step 8. Mark the ticket complete once Step 2 succeeds.

RB-4. Scheduled retention enforcement
  - accounts-db: a nightly job deletes accounts closed more than 24 months ago. Job has been failing since a schema change; see JIRA OPS-4471, open for 7 months.
  - txn-store: no deletion job. Data is retained indefinitely.
  - eventlake: lifecycle rule deletes partitions older than 13 months. Verified working.
  - searchidx: rebuilt weekly from accounts-db, so deletions propagate within 7 days.
  - logs-hot / logs-cold: index lifecycle management, 30 days and 18 months respectively.
  - supportdesk: vendor default is indefinite retention. No configuration applied.
  - mailer: 24-month inactivity purge configured.

RB-5. Backups
  Backups of accounts-db and txn-store are taken nightly, encrypted, and retained 35 days. Additionally, a quarterly 'compliance snapshot' of both databases is taken and retained for seven years in cold storage for audit purposes. This is not covered by the 35-day rule.

RB-6. Known gaps
  - The hashed user id in eventlake uses SHA-256 of the email address with no salt.
  - The datawarehouse retains a copy of accounts-db including deleted rows because the ETL is append-only with a valid_from/valid_to model.

================ END OF MATERIALS ================

Deliver a compliance gap analysis:

1. A findings register. Each finding must have: an ID, a one-line title, the conflicting or non-compliant condition, the specific citations (e.g. 'Doc A 3.9 vs Doc B Art 17(3)'), a severity (Critical / High / Medium / Low) with justification, and the affected systems from Doc C RB-2. Find at least twelve findings. At least four must be genuine three-way conflicts or gaps that only appear when all three documents are read together.
2. Direct contradictions between Doc A and Doc B. There are several; list them all, quote both sides, and state which governs and why.
3. The pseudonymisation question. Doc C RB-3 Step 4 relies on a claim about eventlake. Evaluate that claim against Doc A 2.2, Doc B Article 21, and Doc C RB-6. Rule on whether eventlake data is Personal Data, Pseudonymised Data, or Anonymised Data, and explain the consequence for the erasure obligation. Be specific about why the unsalted hash matters and what an attacker would actually do.
4. Timeline arithmetic. Trace a single erasure request end to end through Doc C RB-3, adding up the worst-case elapsed time for each system, and compare against Doc A 4.1 and Doc B Article 17(1) and 17(2). Produce a table of system, worst-case days to erasure, and compliant yes/no. State the total worst case and name the systems that blow the deadline.
5. The backup problem. Doc A 4.4 says deletion from backups is not performed. Doc B Article 17(3) permits an alternative. State exactly what Doc A would have to say to be compliant, and then evaluate Doc C RB-5's 'compliance snapshot' against that standard - it is materially worse than the 35-day backup issue, and you should explain why in terms of the specific obligations.
6. Doc A 3.5 requires pseudonymisation of security logs after 90 days. Doc C makes no mention of this. State the gap, and then evaluate whether Doc A 3.5 would even be sufficient under Doc B Article 21 if it were implemented.
7. The retention-schedule conflicts. Build a table of every data category in Doc A section 3, the retention period Doc A states, the period actually implemented per Doc C, and the period Doc B would permit. Flag every row where the three disagree. Note that for at least one category Doc C retains data forever with no policy basis at all.
8. A remediation plan of at most fifteen items, each with owner role, effort (S/M/L), risk reduced, and dependency ordering. Put anything that is a live regulatory exposure at the top and say why.
9. Finally: if a supervisory authority audited tomorrow, name the single finding most likely to result in a penalty, quote the exact provision it breaches, and draft the three-sentence disclosure you would make.

prompts.title: Root cause from raw evidence
prompts.text:
An engineer has drafted a postmortem. Attached to it are the raw metric dumps and the configuration diffs from the incident window. The draft's conclusion is not supported by the evidence. Work out what actually happened.

================ ARTEFACT 1: POSTMORTEM DRAFT (unedited) ================

Title: API latency degradation, 14:02-15:41
Author: on-call engineer, first draft

Summary: A memory leak in the api-gateway service caused garbage-collection pauses which increased p99 latency from 180 ms to 4.2 s. Restarting the gateway fleet resolved the issue. Root cause is the memory leak introduced in gateway v2.19.0.

Detail: At 14:02 our latency alert fired. Investigation showed api-gateway heap usage climbing steadily. GC time per minute rose from 40 ms to 900 ms. We restarted the fleet at 15:38 and latency recovered by 15:41. The gateway had been deployed at 09:15 that morning with v2.19.0, which added the new request-tagging feature. We believe the tagging feature retains request objects.

prompts.title: Critical synthesis of five studies
prompts.text:
Five paper abstracts, a benchmark table, and a reproduction report follow. They concern the same question and they do not agree. Read everything, then write the synthesis described at the end. Cite by paper label for every claim.

================ PAPER P1 ================
Title: Speculative Prefetching Restores Throughput in Disaggregated KV Stores
Venue: SysConf, two years ago. Authors: Lund, Aritzeta, Ko.
Abstract: Disaggregating memory from compute in key-value stores has been reported to cost 3-5x in tail latency. We show that most of this cost is attributable to serialized dependent lookups rather than to network round-trip time itself. We present SPECTRA, a speculative prefetcher that issues predicted follow-on reads before the current read completes, using a learned index over the access graph. On our 40-node testbed with 100 Gb/s RDMA, SPECTRA recovers 82% of the throughput lost to disaggregation on YCSB-C and reduces p99 latency from 340 us to 118 us. We report a 9% increase in network traffic and a 4% increase in CPU utilization. We conclude that disaggregation is practical for read-heavy workloads.

================ PAPER P2 ================
Title: A Critical Look at Speculative Prefetching Under Realistic Skew
Venue: SysConf, one year ago. Authors: Beaumont, Xi.
Abstract: We reproduce SPECTRA (P1) and evaluate it under access distributions drawn from three production traces rather than the uniform and Zipf-0.99 distributions used in the original work. Under production skew (fitted Zipf exponents 1.31, 1.47, and 0.62 respectively), speculative prefetching recovers between 11% and 71% of lost throughput, with the low end corresponding to the most skewed trace. We identify the cause: the learned index achieves 0.91 top-1 accuracy on synthetic Zipf-0.99 but only 0.44 on the most skewed production trace, because the access graph is dominated by a small set of hot keys whose successors are effectively random. We further observe that mispredicted prefetches consume the same network capacity as useful ones, so at 0.44 accuracy the network overhead is 61%, not 9%. We do not dispute P1's numbers on their own workloads.

================ PAPER P3 ================
Title: FARLINE: Bounded-Staleness Caching Beats Speculation
Venue: OSSymp, one year ago. Authors: Ndiaye, Trevisan, Ohashi, Bell.
Abstract: We argue that the correct response to disaggregation latency is caching with bounded staleness rather than speculation. FARLINE maintains a compute-local cache with a configurable staleness bound and a lease protocol that guarantees linearizability for reads that observe a valid lease. On a 64-node cluster with 200 Gb/s RDMA we recover 94% of the throughput lost to disaggregation on YCSB-B at a staleness bound of 5 ms, and 71% at a bound of 0 ms (i.e. strict linearizability). We compare against SPECTRA and observe a 2.1x throughput advantage. We note that our testbed uses 200 Gb/s networking versus SPECTRA's 100 Gb/s and that we did not re-tune SPECTRA's learned index for our traces.

================ PAPER P4 ================
Title: On the Reproducibility of Disaggregated Memory Results
Venue: RepliCon, six months ago. Authors: Kirchner, Mbeki, Sato, Larsson, Duval.
Abstract: We attempt to reproduce the headline results of eleven papers on disaggregated memory published in the last three years, including P1 and P3. Artifacts were available for eight. We successfully reproduce the qualitative direction of the result in seven of eight cases but reproduce the quantitative headline number within 10% in only two. The most common causes of divergence are: undocumented NIC firmware versions (5 of 8), a difference between reported and actual working-set size (4 of 8), and reporting p99 over a window that excludes a warm-up period whose length is not stated (6 of 8). For P1 we measure 63% throughput recovery versus the reported 82% on what we believe is an equivalent configuration; the authors attribute the gap to NIC firmware and we were unable to obtain the original firmware. For P3 we measure 88% versus the reported 94% at a 5 ms staleness bound, which we consider a successful reproduction. We recommend that the community require firmware and warm-up disclosure.

================ PAPER P5 ================
Title: The Network Is Not the Bottleneck: A Measurement Study
Venue: NetMeas, four months ago. Authors: Aritzeta, Ko, Prendergast.
Abstract: Prior work on disaggregated memory, including our own (P1), has assumed that the dominant cost is network round-trip time. Using hardware counters on a 96-node deployment, we show that for realistic object sizes (median 340 bytes) the dominant cost is instead the per-request software path: 61% of end-to-end latency is spent in the RDMA verbs library and the memory registration path, and only 24% is time on the wire. We show that a batching layer that amortizes the software path across 8 requests reduces p99 by 44% with no speculation and no caching. We further show that SPECTRA's gains on our original testbed are largely explained by incidental batching in its prefetch issue path rather than by prediction accuracy: disabling prediction but retaining the batched issue path recovers 71% of the 82% figure reported in P1. We consider this a partial retraction of P1's causal claim.

================ BENCHMARK TABLE (compiled by an independent third party) ================

SPECTRA |  40           | 100      | trace-A    | 1.31 | 1 KiB    | 11%                 | 511    | 61%              | P2
SPECTRA |  40           | 100      | trace-B    | 1.47 | 1 KiB    | 19%                 | 470    | 58%              | P2

================ REPRODUCTION REPORT (excerpt, from the P4 artifact evaluation committee) ================

On P1: the artifact builds and runs. The evaluation script defaults to a 60-second run with no warm-up flag; the paper states p99 over 'steady state'. Setting a 120-second warm-up changes the reported p99 from 118 us to 143 us on the authors' own hardware. The working-set size in the script is 12 GiB; the paper says 'approximately 16 GiB'. At 16 GiB the recovery figure falls to 74%.

On P3: the artifact includes a Dockerfile and pinned firmware. Results reproduce within 7%. The lease protocol's fast path is only exercised when the staleness bound exceeds the measured clock skew; the script sets clock skew to 0 via a mocked clock. With a 1.2 ms simulated skew, the 0 ms staleness result falls from 71% to 58%.

On the comparison in P3 against SPECTRA: the SPECTRA configuration used has the learned index trained on YCSB-C and evaluated on YCSB-B. The P1 authors state this is not a supported configuration.

================ END OF MATERIALS ================

Write a critical synthesis. Requirements:

1. State the question all five papers are trying to answer, in one sentence, and then state precisely how each paper's question differs from that shared question. At least two papers are answering a subtly different question than they appear to; identify them.
2. Build an evidence table for the central claim 'speculative prefetching substantially recovers throughput lost to disaggregation'. Rows: each independent piece of evidence. Columns: source, direction of support, effect size, the confound that limits it, and your weighting of its credibility with a justification. Do not treat all sources as equally strong.
3. Resolve the P1 versus P2 conflict. Both report numbers for SPECTRA on the same hardware. Explain why both can be correct, identify the single variable that explains the whole spread from 11% to 82%, and state the condition under which SPECTRA is worth deploying. Give the condition quantitatively using the numbers available.
4. Resolve the P1 versus P5 conflict. P5 shares two authors with P1 and calls itself a partial retraction. Determine what exactly is retracted and what is not. Compute, from the table, how much of P1's headline is attributable to prediction versus to incidental batching, and state the arithmetic.
5. Adjudicate the P3 versus P1 comparison. P3 claims a 2.1x advantage over SPECTRA. List every reason from the materials why that comparison is not sound, and estimate what a fair comparison would show, stating clearly which quantities you must assume and how sensitive your estimate is to them.
6. The reproduction report reveals three methodological problems that affect the headline numbers. For each: name it, state the corrected number, and say whether it changes the qualitative conclusion or only the magnitude.
7. Apply P4's finding about warm-up and working-set size to the benchmark table. Recompute SPECTRA's YCSB-C recovery figure with both corrections applied, showing your reasoning, and state the uncertainty range you would attach to it. Then say which row of the benchmark table you consider the single most trustworthy and why.
8. Write the paragraph you would put in a related-work section of your own paper summarizing this literature honestly in under 150 words, with citations, that does not overstate any result.
9. Finally, design the experiment that would settle the question. Specify: the hypothesis, the independent variables and their levels, the controls (naming the specific confounds from P4 and the reproduction report that you are controlling for), the metrics, the number of runs and the statistical test, and the result that would falsify each of the three competing positions (P1's, P3's, and P5's). Be concrete enough that someone could run it.
